CHAPTER 5 Genes and Human Diseases 123
In these scenarios, individuals have an altered copy number of a
region that may encompass many genes. While some chromosomal
disorders are heritable, many spontaneously arise in the germline or
early in development. Of the myriad of possible chromosomal disorders, only a small fraction is compatible with life and present medically. Many early spontaneous pregnancy losses are attributable to
chromosomal disorders.
• Complex multigenic disorders. They are most often caused by
interactions between multiple genetic variants and environmental factors. Many of these variants are common alleles within the
population and are called polymorphisms. Each causative variant
associated with disease is inherited together with other nearby
polymorphisms as a risk haplotype. In contrast to monogenic
disorders where mutations demonstrate high penetrance (e.g.,
the highly increased cancer risk seen in Li-Fraumeni syndrome
patients with TP53 mutations), in complex multigenic disorders,
risk conferred by any single haplotype is low, and susceptibility
is attributed to the additive effects of several such polymorphisms—hence the term multigenic or polygenic. Since environmental interactions are also important in the pathogenesis of these
diseases, they are also called multifactorial disorders. In this category are some of the most common diseases that afflict humans,
including atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, autoimmune diseases, and cancers. Additionally, normal traits including
height and weight are affected by inherited genetic variants.
In addition to monogenic, complex multigenic, and chromosomal
disorders, a fourth category of genetic disorders stemming from somatically acquired mutations is increasingly recognized. Some somatically acquired mutations “drive” malignancies and are considered in
other chapters. Others contribute to clonal selection and manifest as
precancerous conditions, like clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate
potential (CHIP), which has been associated with risk not only for
evolution to hematologic cancers but also for the development of cardiovascular disease. Still other somatically acquired mutations can
cause overgrowth syndromes, which we will review in this chapter.
We start our discussion with mutations that affect single genes,
which underlie Mendelian disorders, followed by transmission patterns and selected examples of single-gene disorders.
Mutations
A mutation is defined as a permanent change in DNA sequence.
Mutations transmitted by germ cells to progeny can give rise to inherited diseases. Mutations that arise in somatic cells understandably
do not cause hereditary diseases.
Gene mutations can be grouped into several categories depending
on their location and their precise nature:

in which a single nucleotide base pair is substituted with a different
base pair. It may alter the code in a triplet of bases and lead to the replacement of one amino acid by another. Such mutations alter the
sequence of the encoded protein and are termed missense mutations.
If the substituted amino acid is biochemically similar to the original,
it may cause little change in the function of the protein, and the mutation is called a “conservative” missense mutation. On the other hand,
a “nonconservative” missense mutation replaces the normal amino
acid with a biochemically different one. An example of this type is the
sickle cell anemia mutation affecting the β-globin chain of hemoglobin (Chapter 14). Here the nucleotide triplet CTC (or GAG in mRNA,
which encodes glutamic acid) is changed to CAC (or GUG in mRNA,
which encodes valine). This single amino acid substitution promotes
abnormal hemoglobin polymerization, giving rise to sickle cell
anemia. Besides producing an amino acid substitution, a point mutation may change an amino acid codon to a chain-terminating stop
codon (nonsense mutation). Taking again the example of β-globin, a
point mutation affecting the codon for glutamine (CAG) creates a
stop codon (UAG) if U is substituted for C (Fig. 5.1). This change leads

result from mutations outside of exons. Recall that transcription of

point mutations within introns may lead to defective mRNA splicing.
This interferes with normal processing of the pre-mRNA transcripts
and a failure to form the protein-coding mature mRNA. The resulting transcripts may be degraded or nonfunctional, and as a result, the
encoded protein product is not synthesized.

the coding sequence can have two effects on the encoded protein.

the reading frame remains intact, and an abnormal protein lacking

will result in an alteration of the reading frame, producing what is
referred to as a frameshift (Figs. 5.3 and 5.4). Typically, the resulting
RNA encodes a variable number of incorrect amino acids followed

alteration, such as copy number changes—amplifications or deletions—or rearrangements that result in aberrant gain or loss of protein
function. As with other types of mutations, structural changes may

tissues. An example of a pathogenic germline alteration involving a
contiguous interval of a chromosome rather than a single gene is the

• Trinucleotide-repeat mutations. Trinucleotide-repeat mutations
comprise a special category of genetic anomaly. These mutations
are characterized by amplifications of simple tandem repeat sequences of three nucleotides. For example, in fragile X syndrome
(FXS), there are 250 to 4000 tandem repeats of the sequence CGG
within a regulatory region of the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1) gene. In normal populations, the number of repeats is

dynamic. The size and instability of the expanded repeat influences
the phenotypic manifestations of the allele, as we will consider later.
To summarize, mutations can interfere with gene function at many
levels. Transcription may be compromised by gene deletions and mutations involving promoter sequences. Abnormal mRNA processing
may result from mutations affecting splice junctions. Translation may
be prematurely truncated by a nonsense mutation or a frameshift
mutation introducing a stop codon. Finally, pathogenic point mutations may also lead to production of a dysfunctional protein.

of genetic disorders: (1) Mendelian disorders related to single-gene mutations, (2) complex multigenic diseases with multifactorial inheritance,

influenced by genomic imprinting or gonadal mosaicism. Finally, we
will consider a fifth group, conditions caused by somatic mosaicism.

definition, are transmitted in the germline through generations and

• Structural alterations in protein-coding genes. In addition to discrete changes in DNA sequence, coding genes also can undergo structural alteration, such as copy number changes—amplifications or deletions—or rearrangements that result in aberrant gain or loss of protein function. As with other types of mutations, structural changes may occur in the germline and be heritable or can be acquired in somatic tissues. An example of a pathogenic germline alteration involving a contiguous interval of a chromosome rather than a single gene is the 22q microdeletion syndrome, discussed later. Cancers often contain somatically acquired structural alterations; the Philadelphia chromosome translocation t(9;22) between the BCR and ABL genes in chronic myeloid leukemia (Chapter 13) is a classic example.

• Trinucleotide-repeat mutations. Trinucleotide-repeat mutations comprise a special category of genetic anomaly. These mutations are characterized by amplifications of simple tandem repeat sequences of three nucleotides. For example, in fragile X syndrome (FXS), there are 250 to 4000 tandem repeats of the sequence CGG within a regulatory region of the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1) gene. In normal populations, the number of repeats is small, averaging 29. Expansions of the trinucleotide-repeat sequence prevent normal expression of the FMR1 gene. Another distinguishing feature of trinucleotide-repeat mutations is that they are dynamic. The size and instability of the expanded repeat influences the phenotypic manifestations of the allele, as we will consider later. To summarize, mutations can interfere with gene function at many levels. Transcription may be compromised by gene deletions and mutations involving promoter sequences. Abnormal mRNA processing may result from mutations affecting splice junctions. Translation may be prematurely truncated by a nonsense mutation or a frameshift mutation introducing a stop codon. Finally, pathogenic point mutations may also lead to production of a dysfunctional protein. With this background, we now turn our attention to different categories of genetic disorders: (1) Mendelian disorders related to single-gene mutations, (2) complex multigenic diseases with multifactorial inheritance, (3) chromosomal disorders, and (4) single-gene disorders with nonclassical patterns of inheritance. This heterogeneous group includes disorders resulting from triplet-repeat mutations, those arising from mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), and those in which the transmission is influenced by genomic imprinting or gonadal mosaicism. Finally, we will consider a fifth group, conditions caused by somatic mosaicism. Some fundamentals on DNA structure and gene regulation are described in Chapter 1. It is important to clarify commonly used terms—hereditary, familial, and congenital. Hereditary disorders, by definition, are transmitted in the germline through generations and therefore are familial. The term congenital simply means “born with.” Some congenital diseases are not genetic (e.g., congenital syphilis). Not all genetic diseases are congenital; individuals with Huntington disease, for example, begin to manifest their condition in adulthood. SINGLE-GENE DISORDERS Single-gene or monogenic disorders result from mutations that have large functional effects and manifest in families with Mendelian inheritance patterns. Many mutations in autosomal genes produce no phenotype or a muted phenotype in individuals heterozygous for the mutation while affecting homozygotes more severely. Asymptomatic carriers are typical for loss-of-function mutations in genes that do not display haploinsufficiency (i.e., autosomal genes for which one functional allele is sufficient, asymptomatic carriers are typically observed. Although Mendelian traits are usually described as dominant or recessive, in some cases both maternal and paternal alleles contribute to the phenotype—a condition called codominance. Histocompatibility and AB blood group antigens are good examples of codominant inheritance.

A single mutation may lead to many end effects, a phenomenon termed pleiotropism; conversely, mutations at several genetic loci may produce the same phenotype, a phenomenon known as genetic heterogeneity. Sickle cell anemia is an example of pleiotropism. In this hereditary disorder, not only does the point mutation in the gene give rise to HbS, which predisposes red cells to hemolysis, but also the abnormal red cells tend to cause a logjam in small vessels, inducing, for example, splenic fibrosis, organ infarcts, and bone changes. The numerous end-organ effects are all related to the primary defect in hemoglobin synthesis. CHAPTER 5 Genes and Human Diseases 125
apparently homogeneous clinical entity, can result from autosomal
recessive mutations in many different genes.
Transmission Patterns of Single-Gene Disorders
Disorders caused by mutations involving single genes typically follow one of three patterns of inheritance: autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked. Our readers will recall the general rules
that govern the transmission of single-gene disorders; a high-level
summary is included here. Single-gene disorders departing from these
classic patterns of inheritance are described later in the chapter.
Autosomal Dominant Disorders
Autosomal dominant disorders are manifested in the heterozygous
state, such that one parent of an index case is usually affected. Both
males and females are affected, and both can transmit the condition.
When an affected and an unaffected person reproduce, each child has
one chance in two of inheriting the mutated allele from the affected
parent and developing the disease. However, there are some exceptions
to these basic rules:
• Patients may not have an affected parent if their condition is caused by a
new (de novo) germline mutation. The proportion of patients who develop the disease because of a new mutation is related to the effect of the
disease on reproductive capability. If a disease markedly reduces reproductive fitness, more cases result from new mutations. In some instances,
new mutations are known to have a propensity to occur in germ cells of
relatively older fathers (e.g., mutations affecting receptor tyrosine kinase
[RTK]-RAS-MAPK pathway genes, including mutations in fibroblast
growth factor receptor 2 [FGFR2] and FGFR3, which cause Apert syndrome and achondroplasia, respectively, in offspring).
• Patients may not have an affected parent if the disease is partially penetrant. Some individuals inherit the mutant gene but are phenotypically
normal. This is referred to as incomplete penetrance. Penetrance is expressed in mathematical terms. Thus, 50% penetrance indicates that
50% of those who carry the gene express the trait. In contrast to penetrance, if a trait is manifest in all individuals carrying the mutant gene
at differing degrees of severity, the phenomenon is called variable expressivity. For example, the phenotype of neurofibromatosis type 1
ranges from brownish spots on the skin to multiple skin tumors and
skeletal deformities. The mechanisms underlying incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity are not fully understood; effects of
other genes (genetic modifiers) or environmental factors may play
roles. For example, the phenotype of a patient with sickle cell anemia
(resulting from mutation at the β-globin locus) is modified by the
genotype at the HbF locus because this influences whether there is
persistent expression of fetal hemoglobin (Chapter 14). The influence
of environmental factors is exemplified by individuals heterozygous for
familial hypercholesterolemia (FH). The expression of the disease in
the form of atherosclerosis is influenced by dietary intake of lipids.
• In some conditions, the age at onset is delayed; symptoms and signs
may not appear until adulthood (as in Huntington disease).
The molecular mechanisms of autosomal dominant disorders
depend on the nature of the mutation and the type of protein affected. Some mutations, termed loss-of-function mutations, lead to reduced production of a gene product or give rise to a dysfunctional or
inactive protein. Whether such a mutation gives rise to dominant or
recessive disease depends on whether the remaining copy of the gene
is capable of compensating for the loss. In the instance of an autosomal
dominant inheritance pattern, a normal allele (wild-type allele) cannot
compensate for a loss-of-function mutant, a circumstance called haploinsufficiency. Mutations in the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor are one such example; in FH, discussed later, a 50% reduction of
LDL receptors results in elevations of cholesterol that, in turn, promote
atherosclerosis in affected heterozygotes.
For some mutations, especially in structural genes encoding subunit(s)
of multimeric protein complexes, heterozygosity for a mutant allele has a
dominant negative effect. That is, the abnormal protein interferes with the
assembly of functional multimers of the normal protein. For example, the
collagen molecule is a trimer in which the three collagen chains are arranged in a helical configuration. Each of the three collagen chains in the
helix must be normal for the proper assembly and stability of the collagen
molecule. Thus, even with a single mutant collagen chain, normal collagen trimers cannot form. This effect is illustrated by some forms of osteogenesis imperfecta, characterized by marked deficiency of collagen and
severe skeletal abnormalities (Chapter 26).
Finally, and less commonly, there are gain-of-function mutations,
which can take two forms. Some mutations result in an increase in
normal function of a protein, for example, excessive enzymatic activity.
In other cases, mutations impart a wholly new activity completely unrelated to the affected protein’s normal function (i.e., a neomorphic
allele). The transmission of gain-of-function mutations is often autosomal dominant, as illustrated by Huntington disease (Chapter 28). In
this disease the trinucleotide-repeat mutation affecting the Huntington
gene gives rise to an abnormal protein, called huntingtin, that is toxic
to neurons, and hence heterozygotes develop a neurologic deficit.
Table 5.1 lists common autosomal dominant disorders. Many are
considered in other chapters. Some illustrative examples not considered elsewhere are discussed later in this chapter.
Autosomal Recessive Disorders
In autosomal recessive traits, both alleles of an autosomal gene
must be be mutated in order to produce a phenotypic manifestation. They make up the largest category of Mendelian disorders and
are characterized by the following features: (1) The trait does not usually affect the parents of the affected individual (i.e., they “skip generations”), but siblings may show the disease; and (2) siblings have
one chance in four of having the trait (i.e., the recurrence risk is 25%
for each birth). Sometimes, affected individuals inherit two distinct
loss-of-function mutations; these individuals are compound heterozygotes. In other instances, the same mutant allele is inherited both
maternally and paternally. If the mutation occurs with a low allele
frequency in the general population, there is a strong likelihood that
the affected homozygous individual (proband) is the product of a
consanguineous marriage. The features that generally apply to most

Transmission Patterns of Single-Gene Disorders
Disorders caused by mutations involving single genes typically fol-

that govern the transmission of single-gene disorders; a high-level
summary is included here. Single-gene disorders departing from these
classic patterns of inheritance are described later in the chapter.
Autosomal Dominant Disorders
Autosomal dominant disorders are manifested in the heterozygous
state, such that one parent of an index case is usually affected. Both
males and females are affected, and both can transmit the condition.
When an affected and an unaffected person reproduce, each child has
one chance in two of inheriting the mutated allele from the affected
parent and developing the disease. However, there are some exceptions
to these basic rules:
• Patients may not have an affected parent if their condition is caused by a
new (de novo) germline mutation. The proportion of patients who de-
velop the disease because of a new mutation is related to the effect of the
disease on reproductive capability. If a disease markedly reduces repro-
ductive fitness, more cases result from new mutations. In some instances,
new mutations are known to have a propensity to occur in germ cells of
relatively older fathers (e.g., mutations affecting receptor tyrosine kinase
[RTK]-RAS-MAPK pathway genes, including mutations in fibroblast
growth factor receptor 2 [FGFR2] and FGFR3, which cause Apert syn-
drome and achondroplasia, respectively, in offspring).
• Patients may not have an affected parent if the disease is partially pene-
trant. Some individuals inherit the mutant gene but are phenotypically
normal. This is referred to as incomplete penetrance. Penetrance is ex-
pressed in mathematical terms. Thus, 50% penetrance indicates that
50% of those who carry the gene express the trait. In contrast to pen-
etrance, if a trait is manifest in all individuals carrying the mutant gene
at differing degrees of severity, the phenomenon is called variable ex-
pressivity. For example, the phenotype of neurofibromatosis type 1
ranges from brownish spots on the skin to multiple skin tumors and
skeletal deformities. The mechanisms underlying incomplete pene-
trance and variable expressivity are not fully understood; effects of
other genes (genetic modifiers) or environmental factors may play
roles. For example, the phenotype of a patient with sickle cell anemia
(resulting from mutation at the b-globin locus) is modified by the
genotype at the HbF locus because this influences whether there is
persistent expression of fetal hemoglobin (Chapter 14). The influence
of environmental factors is exemplified by individuals heterozygous for
familial hypercholesterolemia (FH). The expression of the disease in
the form of atherosclerosis is influenced by dietary intake of lipids.
• In some conditions, the age at onset is delayed; symptoms and signs
may not appear until adulthood (as in Huntington disease).
The molecular mechanisms of autosomal dominant disorders
depend on the nature of the mutation and the type of protein af-
fected. Some mutations, termed loss-of-function mutations, lead to re-
duced production of a gene product or give rise to a dysfunctional or
inactive protein. Whether such a mutation gives rise to dominant or
recessive disease depends on whether the remaining copy of the gene
is capable of compensating for the loss. In the instance of an autosomal
dominant inheritance pattern, a normal allele (wild-type allele) cannot
compensate for a loss-of-function mutant, a circumstance called hap-
loinsufficiency. Mutations in the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) recep-
tor are one such example; in FH, discussed later, a 50% reduction of
LDL receptors results in elevations of cholesterol that, in turn, promote
atherosclerosis in affected heterozygotes.
For some mutations, especially in structural genes encoding subunit(s)
of multimeric protein complexes, heterozygosity for a mutant allele has a
dominant negative effect. That is, the abnormal protein interferes with the
assembly of functional multimers of the normal protein. For example, the
collagen molecule is a trimer in which the three collagen chains are ar-
ranged in a helical configuration. Each of the three collagen chains in the
helix must be normal for the proper assembly and stability of the collagen
molecule. Thus, even with a single mutant collagen chain, normal colla-
gen trimers cannot form. This effect is illustrated by some forms of osteo-
genesis imperfecta, characterized by marked deficiency of collagen and
severe skeletal abnormalities (Chapter 26).
Finally, and less commonly, there are gain-of-function mutations,
which can take two forms. Some mutations result in an increase in
normal function of a protein, for example, excessive enzymatic activity.
In other cases, mutations impart a wholly new activity completely un-
related to the affected protein’s normal function (i.e., a neomorphic
allele). The transmission of gain-of-function mutations is often autoso-
mal dominant, as illustrated by Huntington disease (Chapter 28). In
this disease the trinucleotide-repeat mutation affecting the Huntington
gene gives rise to an abnormal protein, called huntingtin, that is toxic
to neurons, and hence heterozygotes develop a neurologic deficit.

ered elsewhere are discussed later in this chapter.
Autosomal Recessive Disorders
In autosomal recessive traits, both alleles of an autosomal gene
must be be mutated in order to produce a phenotypic manifesta-
tion. They make up the largest category of Mendelian disorders and
are characterized by the following features: (1) The trait does not usu-
ally affect the parents of the affected individual (i.e., they “skip gen-
erations”), but siblings may show the disease; and (2) siblings have
one chance in four of having the trait (i.e., the recurrence risk is 25%
for each birth). Sometimes, affected individuals inherit two distinct
loss-of-function mutations; these individuals are compound heterozy-
gotes. In other instances, the same mutant allele is inherited both
maternally and paternally. If the mutation occurs with a low allele
frequency in the general population, there is a strong likelihood that
the affected homozygous individual (proband) is the product of a
consanguineous marriage. The features that generally apply to most

X-Linked Disorders
X-linked disorders are caused by abnormalities in genes on the X
chromosome, so males are affected whereas females are carriers.
The X chromosome contains many genes without corresponding loci
on the Y chromosome. Mutations in these can give rise to X-linked
recessive inheritance patterns, which accounts for several well-defined
clinical conditions. Females are asymptomatic heterozygote carriers;
affected males are said to be hemizygous for X-linked mutant genes.
In contrast, the male-specific region of the Y chromosome encodes
relatively few genes, most related to spermatogenesis. Males with mu-
tations affecting these Y-linked genes are often infertile, and hence
cannot pass these mutant alleles to offspring. A few Y-linked genes fall
in the “pseudoautosomal” regions of the sex chromosomes, with copies
on both the X and Y chromosomes; rare disorders resulting from mu-
tations in these genes have been described. Features that characterize
X-linked, recessive disorders are:
•  An affected male does not transmit the disorder to his sons (who
instead inherit a paternal Y chromosome); rather, all his daughters
are obligate carriers.
•  Daughters of heterozygous women have one chance in two of
being a carrier. Sons of heterozygous women have one chance in
two of inheriting the mutant allele and being affected by the
disease.

CHAPTER 5 Genes and Human Diseases 127
Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene
(Mendelian) Disorders
Mendelian disorders result from alterations involving single
genes, which may lead to loss of the encoded protein or the formation of an abnormal protein product. Virtually any type of protein
may be affected in single-gene disorders and by a variety of mechanisms (Table 5.4). The pattern of inheritance of the disease is related
to the kind of protein affected by the mutation and the effect of the
mutation. For this discussion, we will consider four categories of
mechanisms involved in single-gene disorders: (1) alterations in
structural proteins; (2) defects in membrane receptors and transport
systems; (3) enzyme defects and their consequences; and (4) mutations resulting in disorders of epigenetic machinery.
Alterations in Structural Proteins
Genetic defects resulting in alterations of nonenzymatic, structural
proteins include osteogenesis imperfecta and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
(EDS) (defects in collagen, Chapter 26); Marfan syndrome (defects in
fibrillin, considered later in this chapter); muscular dystrophies (dystrophin, Chapter 27); and hereditary spherocytosis (spectrin, Chapter 14).
Some disease-causing alleles in this group act in an autosomal dominant manner as defective proteins affecting multimer assemblies;
dystrophin mutations are an exception and are typically X-linked
recessive.
Defects in Receptors and Transport Systems
As we discussed in Chapter 1, numerous biologically important substances are actively transported across the cell membrane. In some
cases, transport is achieved by receptor-mediated endocytosis. A genetic defect in a receptor-mediated transport system is exemplified
by familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), in which reduced synthesis or
function of LDL receptors leads to defective transport of LDL into
the cells and secondarily to excessive cholesterol synthesis by complex intermediary mechanisms. In cystic fibrosis the transport system for chloride and bicarbonate ions in exocrine glands, sweat
ducts, lungs, and pancreas is defective. By complex mechanisms,
impaired anion transport leads to serious injury of the lungs and
pancreas (Chapter 10).
The hemoglobinopathies, including sickle cell disease, are characterized by structural defects in the globin molecule, which is critical, of
course, for oxygen transport. In contrast to these disorders, thalassemias
result from mutations in globin genes that reduce the amount of available α-globin or β-globin chain for tetramer formation (Chapter 14).
Both categories of mutation can exhibit dosage effects.
Enzyme Defects and Their Consequences
Mutations may result in the synthesis of an enzyme with reduced
activity or a reduced amount of a normal enzyme. In either case,
the consequence is an interruption of a metabolic pathway. Fig. 5.5
illustrates a hypothetical example of pathway in which the substrate

CHAPTER ₅ Genes and Human Diseases 127
Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene
(Mendelian) Disorders
Mendelian disorders result from alterations involving single
genes, which may lead to loss of the encoded protein or the forma-
tion of an abnormal protein product. Virtually any type of protein
may be affected in single-gene disorders and by a variety of mecha-
nisms (Table 5.4). The pattern of inheritance of the disease is related
to the kind of protein affected by the mutation and the effect of the
mutation. For this discussion, we will consider four categories of
mechanisms involved in single-gene disorders: (1) alterations in
structural proteins; (2) defects in membrane receptors and transport
systems; (3) enzyme defects and their consequences; and (4) muta-
tions resulting in disorders of epigenetic machinery.
Alterations in Structural Proteins
Genetic defects resulting in alterations of nonenzymatic, structural
proteins include osteogenesis imperfecta and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
(EDS) (defects in collagen, Chapter 26); Marfan syndrome (defects in
fibrillin, considered later in this chapter); muscular dystrophies (dys-
trophin, Chapter 27); and hereditary spherocytosis (spectrin, Chapter 14).
Some disease-causing alleles in this group act in an autosomal domi-
nant manner as defective proteins affecting multimer assemblies;
dystrophin mutations are an exception and are typically X-linked
recessive.
Defects in Receptors and Transport Systems
As we discussed in Chapter 1, numerous biologically important sub-
stances are actively transported across the cell membrane. In some
cases, transport is achieved by receptor-mediated endocytosis. A ge-
netic defect in a receptor-mediated transport system is exemplified
by familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), in which reduced synthesis or
function of LDL receptors leads to defective transport of LDL into
the cells and secondarily to excessive cholesterol synthesis by com-
plex intermediary mechanisms. In cystic fibrosis the transport sys-
tem for chloride and bicarbonate ions in exocrine glands, sweat
ducts, lungs, and pancreas is defective. By complex mechanisms,
impaired anion transport leads to serious injury of the lungs and
pancreas (Chapter 10).
The hemoglobinopathies, including sickle cell disease, are character-
ized by structural defects in the globin molecule, which is critical, of
course, for oxygen transport. In contrast to these disorders, thalassemias
result from mutations in globin genes that reduce the amount of avail-
able a-globin or b-globin chain for tetramer formation (Chapter 14).
Both categories of mutation can exhibit dosage effects.
Enzyme Defects and Their Consequences
Mutations may result in the synthesis of an enzyme with reduced
activity or a reduced amount of a normal enzyme. In either case,
the consequence is an interruption of a metabolic pathway. Fig. 5.5

product by a series of enzymatic reactions. Enzyme defects interrupt specific pathways, which can manifest
with (B) substrate accumulation (galactosemia), (C) end product deficiency (albinism), or (D) overproduction
of intermediates (Lesch-Nyhan). M1, M2, Products of a minor pathway.
is converted by intracellular enzymes, denoted as 1, 2, and 3, into an
end product through intermediates 1 and 2. In this model, the final
product exerts negative feedback control on enzyme 1. A minor
pathway producing small quantities of M1 and M2 also exists. An
enzyme defect in such a pathway may lead to two types of
consequences:
• Accumulation of “upstream” substrates. Depending on the site of the
block, accumulation of the starting substrate may be accompanied by
accumulation of one or both intermediates. Moreover, an increased
concentration of intermediate 2 may “spill over” via the minor pathway and lead to an excess of M1 and M2. Under these conditions,
tissue injury may result if the starting substrate, the intermediates, or
the products of alternative minor pathways are toxic in high concentrations.
For example, in galactosemia, the deficiency of galactose-
1-phosphate uridyltransferase (Chapter 10) leads to galactose
accumulation and consequent tissue damage. Excesses of lysosomal contents caused by deficiency of degradative enzymes are
responsible for a group of diseases generally referred to as lysosomal storage diseases. Failure to inactivate a tissue-damaging
substrate is exemplified by a₁-antitrypsin deficiency. Individuals who have an inherited deficiency of serum a₁-antitrypsin are
unable to inactivate neutrophil elastase in their lungs. Unchecked activity of this protease leads to destruction of elastin
in the walls of lung alveoli, leading eventually to emphysema
(Chapter 15).
• End product deficiencies. An enzyme defect causing a pathway
block may result in a decreased amount of a key end product. For
example, a deficiency of melanin may result from lack of tyrosinase, which is necessary for the biosynthesis of melanin from its
precursor, tyrosine, resulting in the clinical condition called
albinism.
If the end product is a feedback inhibitor of enzymes involved in
the upstream reactions (in Fig. 5.5 it is shown that the product inhibits enzyme 1), the end product deficiency may permit overproduction
of intermediates. A prime example of a disease where this occurs is
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, caused by hypoxanthine-guanine phospho-ribosyltransferase (HPRT) deficiency (Chapter 26).
Certain genetically determined enzyme deficiencies are unmasked
only after exposure of the affected individual to certain drugs. This
special area of genetics, called pharmacogenetics, is of considerable
clinical importance. The classic example of drug-induced toxicity in
the genetically susceptible individual is seen in people deficient for the
enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD). Under normal
conditions, G6PD deficiency does not result in disease, but on administration (for example) of the antimalarial drug primaquine, a severe
hemolytic anemia results (Chapter 14). In recent years an increasing
number of polymorphisms of genes encoding drug-metabolizing
enzymes, transporters, and receptors have been identified. In some
cases, these genetic factors have a major impact on drug sensitivity and
adverse reactions. It is hoped that advances in pharmacogenetics will
increasingly lead to patient-tailored therapy, an example of personalized medicine.
Disorders of Epigenetic Machinery
Several Mendelian disorders of epigenetic machinery are recognized; these typically involve mutations in genes that regulate genome function by “writing,” “erasing,” or “reading” epigenetic
marks (e.g., DNA methylation or posttranslational modifications of
histone proteins), or otherwise remodel chromatin. These mutations have broad consequences on gene expression; most manifest
as autosomal dominant syndromes with neurologic dysfunction
and intellectual disability. Examples include Kabuki syndrome,
Wilson-Turner syndrome, Weaver syndrome, Rubinstein-Taybi
syndrome, and Smith-Magenis syndrome, all of which are caused
by mutations in different genes that regulate the epigenome. Of
these, we will consider Rett syndrome (caused by mutations in
X-linked gene encoding the DNA methyl-CpG reader MECP2)
further in this chapter.

discussed below.
• Fibrillin-1 is the major component of microfibrils found in the ECM
(Chapter 1). Bundles of these microfibrils provide a scaffold on
which tropoelastin is deposited to form elastin fibers. Together,
these ECM structural proteins lend stability and strength to tissues,
and they are particularly important in tissues which undergo
stretch and recoil. The aorta, ligaments, and circumferential ciliary
zonules that support the eye lens are prominently affected in
Marfan syndrome. Fibrillin occurs in two homologous forms, fibrillin-1 and fibrillin-2, encoded by two separate genes, FBN1 and
FBN2, mapped on chromosomes 15q21.1 and 5q23.31, respectively.
Mutations of FBN1 underlie Marfan syndrome; mutations of the
related FBN2 gene are less common, and they give rise to congenital
contractural arachnodactyly, an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by skeletal abnormalities. Mutational analysis has revealed
close to 1000 distinct mutations of the FBN1 gene in individuals
with Marfan syndrome. Most of these are missense mutations that
give rise to abnormal fibrillin-1. These disrupt normal polymerization of fibrillin fibers (dominant negative effect). Less commonly,
the reduction of fibrillin content below a certain threshold weakens
the connective tissue (haploinsufficiency, 10% to 15% of cases).
• TGF-β bioavailability. While many clinical manifestations of
Marfan syndrome can be explained by changes in the mechanical
properties of the extracellular matrix resulting from abnormalities of fibrillin, several others such as bone overgrowth and myxoid changes in mitral valves cannot be attributed to changes in
tissue elasticity. It is now known that fibrillin-1 controls TGF-β
bioavailability. Reduced or altered forms of fibrillin-1 give rise to
excessive activation of TGF-β, since normal microfibrils sequester TGF-β. Excessive TGF-β signaling, in turn, has deleterious
effects on vascular smooth muscle development, and increases
the activity of metalloproteases (MMPs), causing loss of extracellular matrix. This schema is supported by the observation that
gain-of-function mutations in the TGF-β type II receptor give
rise to a related syndrome, called Marfan syndrome type 2
(MFS2). Furthermore, patients with germline mutations in one

isoform of TGF-β, called TGF-b3, present with an inherited
predisposition to aortic aneurysm and other cardiovascular
manifestations like those found in patients with classic Marfan
syndrome.
MORPHOLOGY
Skeletal abnormalities are the most striking feature of Marfan syndrome. Patients are typically unusually tall with long extremities and long,
tapering fingers and toes. The joint ligaments in the hands and feet are lax,
suggesting that the patient is double-jointed; typically the thumb can be hyper-extended back to the wrist. The head is commonly dolichocephalic (long
headed) with bossing of the frontal eminences and prominent supraorbital
ridges. A variety of spinal deformities may appear, including kyphosis, scoliosis, or rotation or slipping of the dorsal or lumbar vertebrae. The chest is
classically deformed, presenting either pectus excavatum (deeply depressed
sternum) or a pigeon-breast deformity.
Ocular changes take many forms. Most characteristic is bilateral subluxation or dislocation (usually outward and upward) of the lens, referred to as
ectopia lentis. This abnormality, resulting from weakening of ciliary zonules, is
so uncommon in persons who do not have this disease that the finding of bilateral ectopia lentis should raise the suspicion of Marfan syndrome.

in 40% to 50% of cases and, of greater importance, dilation of the ascending
aorta due to medial degeneration (Chapter 12). Loss of medial support results
in progressive dilation of the aortic valve ring and the root of the aorta, giving
rise to severe aortic incompetence. Weakening of the media predisposes to an
intimal tear, which may initiate an intramural hematoma that cleaves the lay-
ers of the media to produce aortic dissection. After cleaving the aortic layers
for considerable distances, sometimes back to the root of the aorta or down to
the iliac arteries, the hemorrhage often ruptures through the aortic wall.
Clinical Features
Although mitral valve lesions are more frequent, they are clinically less
important than aortic lesions. Loss of connective tissue support in the
mitral valve leaflets makes them soft and billowy, creating a so-called
floppy valve (Chapter 12). Valvular lesions, along with lengthening of
the chordae tendineae, frequently give rise to mitral regurgitation.
Similar changes may affect the tricuspid and, rarely, the aortic valves.
Echocardiography greatly enhances the ability to detect cardiovascular
abnormalities and is therefore extremely valuable in the diagnosis of
Marfan syndrome. The great majority of deaths are caused by rupture
of aortic dissections, followed in importance by cardiac failure.
While the lesions just described typify Marfan syndrome, it must
be emphasized that there is great variation in the clinical expression
of this genetic disorder. Patients with prominent eye or cardiovascu-
lar changes may have few skeletal abnormalities, whereas others with
striking changes in body habitus have no eye changes. Although vari-
ability in clinical expression may be seen within a family, interfamil-
ial variability is much more common and extensive. This variability
in clinical manifestations is partly attributable to the many different
mutations that affect the fibrillin locus, which number around 1000.
Because of this, the clinical diagnosis of Marfan syndrome is cur-
rently based on the so-called revised Ghent criteria. These incorpo-
rate family history, cardinal clinical signs in the absence of family
history, and presence or absence of fibrillin mutation. In general,

Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome
EDS comprises a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of
disorders that result from a set of mutations in genes that encode
collagen, enzymes that modify collagen, and less commonly other
proteins present in the extracellular matrix. Other disorders result-
ing from mutations affecting collagen synthesis include osteogenesis
imperfecta (Chapter 26), Alport syndrome (Chapter 20), and epider-
molysis bullosa (Chapter 25).
Biosynthesis of collagen is a complex process (Chapter 1) that can
be disturbed by mutations affecting any one of the numerous struc-
tural  collagen  genes  or  enzymes  necessary  for  posttranscriptional
modifications of collagen. Hence EDS is transmitted with both autoso-
mal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance patterns. The 2017
International Classification for the Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes recog-
nizes 13 subtypes, listed in Table 5.5. Although individually rare, the
collective frequency of EDS is 1 in 5000 births. It is beyond the scope
of this book to discuss each variant individually; instead, the important
clinical features common to most variants are summarized, and clini-
cal manifestations are correlated with the underlying molecular defects
in collagen synthesis or structure.
As might be expected, tissues rich in collagen, such as skin,
ligaments, and joints, are involved in most variants of EDS. Be-
cause the abnormal collagen fibers lack adequate tensile strength, skin
is hyperextensible, and the joints are hypermobile. These features per-
mit abnormal ranges of motion, such as bending the thumb backward
to touch the forearm and bending the knee forward to create almost a
right angle. It is believed that many contortionists have one of the
various types of EDS. These individuals are predisposed to joint dis-
locations. The skin is extraordinarily stretchable, extremely fragile, and
easily bruised. Minor injuries produce gaping defects, and surgical

CHAPTER 5 Genes and Human Diseases 131
repair or intervention is accomplished with great difficulty because of
the lack of normal tensile strength. The underlying defect in connective
tissue may lead to serious internal complications. These include rupture
of the colon and large arteries (vascular EDS), ocular fragility with
rupture of cornea and retinal detachment (kyphoscoliosis EDS), and
diaphragmatic hernia (classic EDS).
The genetic bases of these abnormalities are known in all but one
form of EDS—the so-called hypermobility type. Perhaps the best
characterized is the kyphoscoliosis type, the most common autosomal
recessive form of EDS. It results from mutations in the PLOD1 gene
encoding lysyl hydroxylase, an enzyme necessary for hydroxylation of
lysine residues during collagen synthesis. Affected patients have markedly reduced levels of this enzyme. Because hydroxylysine is essential
for intermolecular and intramolecular cross-linking of collagen fibers,
a deficiency of lysyl hydroxylase results in the synthesis of collagen that
lacks normal structural stability.
In the classic type of EDS, mutations in the genes for type V collagen
(COL5A1 and COL5A2) have been detected in most cases. Other extracellular matrix molecules that influence collagen synthesis and assembly may be involved in forms of EDS. One example is a classic-like
EDS caused by mutation in the TNXB gene encoding tenascin X, a
large multimeric protein that interacts with fibrillar types I, III, and V
collagens.
The vascular type of EDS typically results from abnormalities of
type III collagen. It is genetically heterogeneous because at least three
distinct types of mutations affecting the collagen type III gene
(COL3A1) can give rise to vascular EDS. Some affect the rate of synthesis of pro-α1 (III) chains, others affect the secretion of type III
procollagen, and still others lead to the synthesis of structurally abnormal type III collagen. Some mutant alleles behave as dominant negatives (see discussion under “Autosomal Dominant Disorders”) and
thus produce severe phenotypes in heterozygotes. Because blood vessels and intestines are rich in collagen type III, these mutations can
result in severe structural defects (e.g., vulnerability to spontaneous
rupture) in these organs. Unlike other EDS subtypes, the skin is not
usually hyperextensible.
In two forms of EDS—arthrochalasia type and dermatosparaxis
type—the fundamental defect is in the conversion of type I procollagen to collagen. This step in collagen synthesis involves cleavage
and removal of noncollagen domains at the N terminus and C
terminus of the procollagen molecule by N-terminal–specific and
C-terminal–specific peptidases. The defect in the conversion of procollagen to collagen in the arthrochalasia type has been traced to
mutations that affect one of the two type I collagen genes, COL1A1
and COL1A2. As a result, structurally abnormal pro-α1 (I) or pro-α2 (II) chains that resist cleavage of N-terminal peptides are formed.
In patients with a single mutant allele, only 50% of the type I collagen chains are abnormal, but because these chains interfere with the
formation of normal collagen helices, heterozygotes manifest the
disease. In contrast, the related dermatosparaxis type is caused by
mutations in the ADAMTS2 gene that encodes procollagen-N-
peptidase, essential for the cleavage of procollagens. Because in this
case the disease is caused by an enzyme deficiency, it follows an
autosomal recessive form of inheritance.
To summarize, the common thread in EDSs is some abnormality
of collagen. These disorders, however, are extremely heterogeneous. At the molecular level, a myriad of defects, varying from
mutations involving structural genes for collagen to those involving
enzymes that are responsible for posttranslational modifications of
the protein, have been detected. This molecular heterogeneity underlies the clinical variability and different patterns of inheritance
of EDS.
KEY CONCEPTS
Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
Marfan Syndrome
• Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin, which is required for structural integrity of connective tissues and regulation of TGF-β signaling.
• The major tissues affected are the skeleton, eyes, and cardiovascular system.
• Clinical features may include tall stature, long fingers, bilateral subluxation
of lens, mitral valve prolapse, aortic aneurysm, and aortic dissection.
Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
• There are several variants of EDS, all characterized by defects in collagen
synthesis or assembly. Each of the variants is caused by a mutation involving
one of several collagen genes, genes that encode enzymes involved in collagen synthesis, and genes that encode other ECM proteins like tenascin X.
• Clinical features may include fragile, hyperextensible skin vulnerable to
trauma; hypermobile joints; and ruptures involving the colon, cornea, or
large arteries. Wound healing is poor.
Disorders Associated With Defects in Receptor Proteins
Familial Hypercholesterolemia
FH is most commonly caused by mutations in the gene encoding the
receptor for LDL, resulting in inadequate removal of plasma LDL by
the liver. Mutations in the LDL receptor gene (LDLR) account for 80%
to 85% of cases of FH. Most of the remaining cases are caused by mutations in two other genes involved in clearance of plasma LDL. They
encode (1) apolipoprotein B-100 (ApoB), the ligand for LDL receptor
on the LDL particle (5% to 10% of cases), and (2) proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9, 1% to 2% of cases). PCSK9 reduces expression of the LDL receptor by directly binding the protein
and inducing a conformational change marking it for degradation in
lysosomes in lieu of receptor recycling. Each of these three types of
mutations impairs hepatic clearance of LDL and increases serum levels
of cholesterol, giving rise to premature atherosclerosis and a greatly
increased risk of myocardial infarction. The functions of these genes in
cholesterol metabolism are discussed below.
FH caused by LDL receptor mutations is one of the most frequently
occurring Mendelian disorders. Heterozygotes with one mutant gene,
representing about 1 in 200 individuals, have from birth a two- to
three-fold elevation of plasma cholesterol level, leading to tendinous
xanthomas and premature atherosclerosis in adult life (Chapter 11).
Homozygotes, having a double dose of the mutant gene, are much
more severely affected and may have five- to six-fold elevations in
plasma cholesterol levels. Skin xanthomas and coronary, cerebral, and
peripheral vascular atherosclerosis may develop in these individuals at

liver in its synthesis and clearance. Lipolysis of very-low-density lipopro-
tein (VLDL) by lipoprotein lipase in the capillaries releases triglycerides,
which are then stored in fat cells and used as a source of energy in
skeletal  muscles.  ApoB,  Apolipoprotein  B;  ApoC,  apolipoprotein  C;
ApoE, apolipoprotein E; IDL, intermediate-density lipoprotein.
step in this process is the secretion of very-low-density lipoprotein
(VLDL) from the liver into the blood. VLDL particles are rich in triglyc-
erides, and they contain lower amounts of cholesteryl esters. In addition,
they carry apolipoproteins ApoB, ApoC, and ApoE on their surface. In
the capillaries of adipose tissue and muscle, the VLDL particle under-
goes lipolysis and is converted to VLDL remnant, also called interme-
diate-density lipoprotein (IDL). Compared with VLDL, IDL particles
have reduced content of triglycerides and an increase in cholesteryl es-
ters. ApoC is lost, while ApoB and ApoE are retained. After release from
the capillary endothelium, the IDL particles have one of two fates.
Approximately 50% of newly formed IDL is rapidly taken up by the
liver by receptor-mediated transport. The receptor responsible for the
binding of IDL to the liver cell membrane recognizes both ApoB and
ApoE. It is called ApoB/E receptor, or more commonly the LDL recep-
tor, because it is also involved in the hepatic clearance of LDL (described
later). In the liver cells, IDL is recycled to generate VLDL. The IDL
particles not taken up by the liver are subjected to further metabolic
processing that removes most of the remaining triglycerides and ApoE,
yielding ApoB carrying cholesterol-rich LDL particles.
Although  many  cell  types,  including  fibroblasts,  lymphocytes,
smooth muscle cells, hepatocytes, and adrenocortical cells, possess
high-affinity LDL receptors, approximately 70% of the plasma LDL is
cleared by the liver, using a sophisticated transport process (Fig. 5.8).
The first step involves binding of LDL to cell-surface receptors, which
are clustered in specialized regions of the plasma membrane called
coated pits (Chapter 1). After binding, the coated pits containing the
receptor-bound LDL are internalized by clathrin-mediated endocyto-
sis to form coated vesicles, after which they migrate within the cell to
fuse with the lysosomes. Here the LDL dissociates from the receptor,
and the receptor is recycled to the surface. The recycling of LDL recep-
tors is regulated by PCSK9, which binds to LDL receptors on the sur-
face of hepatocytes and causes their degradation after endocytosis. In
the lysosomes, the LDL molecule is enzymatically degraded; the apo-
protein part is hydrolyzed to amino acids, whereas the cholesteryl
esters are broken down to free cholesterol. This free cholesterol, in
turn, crosses the lysosomal membrane to enter the cytoplasm, where it
is  used  for  membrane  synthesis  and  as  a  regulator  of  cholesterol
homeostasis. The exit of cholesterol from the lysosomes requires the
action of two proteins, called NPC1 and NPC2 (see “Niemann-Pick
Disease Type C”). Four separate processes are affected by the released
intracellular cholesterol (see Fig. 5.8):
•  Cholesterol inhibits the enzyme 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coen-
zyme A (HMG CoA) reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in choles-
terol synthesis within the cell.
•  Cholesterol activates the enzyme acyl-coenzyme A:cholesterol ac-
yltransferase, promoting the esterification and storage of excess
cholesterol.
•  Cholesterol suppresses the synthesis of LDL receptors, reducing
cholesterol uptake and accumulation.
•  Cholesterol upregulates the expression of PCSK9, which reduces
recycling of LDL receptors by causing degradation of endocytosed
LDL receptors. This also has the effect of reducing cholesterol up-
take and thus provides an additional mechanism protecting cells
from excessive accumulation of cholesterol.
As mentioned earlier, FH results from mutations in the gene encod-
ing the receptor for LDL or in other genes where mutations compro-
mise LDLR function. The impact of mutations in these genes is:
•  Mutations in the LDLR gene. Heterozygotes with FH due to muta-
tion in the LDLR gene possess only 50% of the normal number of
high-affinity LDL receptors because they have only one functional
allele. As a result of this defect in transport, catabolism of LDL by
the receptor-dependent pathways is impaired, and the plasma level
of LDL increases two- to three-fold. Homozygotes with virtually no
normally functioning LDL receptor have much higher levels of
circulating LDL. In addition to defective LDL clearance, both ho-
mozygotes and heterozygotes have increased synthesis of LDL. The
increased synthesis that contributes to hypercholesterolemia also
results from a lack of LDL receptors. As mentioned above, IDL, the
immediate precursor of plasma LDL, also uses hepatic LDL recep-
tors (apoB/E receptors) for its transport into the liver. In FH, im-
paired IDL transport into the liver secondarily diverts a greater
proportion of plasma IDL into the precursor pool for plasma LDL.
•  Mutations in the gene encoding ApoB. Since ApoB on the surface of
LDL particles is the ligand for LDL receptors, mutations in ApoB
can reduce the binding of LDL molecules with LDL receptors. This
increases serum LDL cholesterol.
•  Activating mutations in the PCSK9 gene. These mutations greatly
reduce the number of LDL receptors on the cell surface due to
increased degradation during the recycling process.
The transport of LDL via the scavenger receptor seems to occur at
least in part into the cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system.

The molecular genetics of FH are extremely complex. More than
2000 mutations involving the LDL receptor gene, including DNA copy
number variations, insertions, deletions, and missense and nonsense
mutations, have been identified. These can be classified into six groups,
five of which are illustrated in Fig. 5.9. Class I mutations are relatively
uncommon and lead to a complete failure of synthesis of the LDL receptor protein (null allele). Class II mutations are fairly common; they
encode LDL receptor proteins that accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum because of C-terminal truncations or folding defects that
block the transport of the mutated receptor proteins to the Golgi
complex. Class III mutations affect the ApoB binding site of the receptor; the mutant LDL receptors reach the cell surface but fail to bind
LDL or do so poorly. Class IV mutations encode LDL receptors that are
synthesized and transported to the cell surface efficiently. They bind
LDL normally, but then fail to localize in coated pits, and hence the
bound LDL is not internalized. Class V mutations encode LDL receptors that are expressed on the cell surface, can bind LDL, and can be
internalized; however, the pH-dependent dissociation of the receptor
and the bound LDL fails to occur. Such receptors are trapped in the
endosome, where they are degraded, and hence they fail to recycle to
the cell surface. Class VI mutations (not shown) were more recently
discovered and disrupt the signaling required for membranous LDL
receptors to be targeted to the basolateral surface of hepatocytes. The
mutated receptors are mistargeted to the apical cell surface, resulting
in poor LDLR exposure to plasma at the sinusoidal interface and reduced endocytosis of LDL.
The discovery of the critical role of LDL receptors in cholesterol
homeostasis has led to the rational design of drugs that lower
plasma cholesterol by increasing the number of LDL receptors. One
strategy is based on the ability of certain drugs (statins) to suppress
intracellular cholesterol synthesis by inhibiting the enzyme HMG CoA
reductase. The reduction in intracellular cholesterol leads to greater
synthesis of LDL receptors by removing the braking action of cholesterol on LDL receptor synthesis. In another strategy, antibodies that
inhibit PCSK9 function reduce the degradation of LDL receptors,
thereby increasing their abundance on the cell membrane and consequently increasing clearance of LDL cholesterol from the blood.

KEY CONCEPTS
Familial Hypercholesterolemia
•  FH is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the genes
encoding the (1) LDL receptor (85% of cases), (2) ApoB protein (5% to 10%
of cases), or (3) PCSK9 (1% to 2% of cases).
•  Patients develop hypercholesterolemia because of impaired LDL uptake by
hepatocytes.
•  In heterozygotes for mutations in the LDLR gene, elevated serum choles-
terol increases the risk of atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease; ho-
mozygotes have an even greater increase in serum cholesterol and a higher
frequency of ischemic heart disease. Cholesterol also deposits along ten-
don sheaths to produce xanthomas.
Disorders Associated With Enzyme Defects
Lysosomal Storage Diseases
Lysosomes are key components of the intracellular digestive system.
They contain a myriad of hydrolytic enzymes, which have two special
properties. First, they function in the acidic milieu of the lysosomes.
Second, these enzymes constitute a special category of secretory pro-
teins that are destined not for the extracellular fluids but for intracel-
lular organelles. This latter characteristic requires special processing
within the Golgi apparatus, which merits brief discussion.
Like other secretory proteins, lysosomal enzymes (or acid hydro-
lases, as they are sometimes called) are synthesized in the endoplasmic
reticulum and transported to the Golgi apparatus. Within the Golgi
complex they undergo a variety of posttranslational modifications in-
cluding the attachment of terminal mannose-6-phosphate groups to
some of the oligosaccharide side chains. The phosphorylated mannose
residues serve as an “address label” that is recognized by specific recep-
tors found on the inner surface of the Golgi membrane. Lysosomal
enzymes bind these receptors and are thereby segregated from the
numerous other secretory proteins within the Golgi. Subsequently,
small transport vesicles containing the receptor-bound enzymes are
pinched off from the Golgi and proceed to fuse with the lysosomes.
After the enzymes are targeted to their intracellular compartment, the
receptors are shuttled back to the Golgi (Fig. 5.10). As indicated later,
genetically determined errors in this sorting mechanism may give rise
to forms of lysosomal storage disease.

may be acquired from outside the cells by phagocytosis (heterophagy).
An inherited deficiency of a functional lysosomal enzyme gives rise to
two pathologic consequences (Fig. 5.11).
• Catabolism of the substrate of the missing enzyme remains incomplete,
leading to the accumulation of the partially degraded insoluble
metabolite within the lysosomes. This is called “primary accumulation.” Stuffed with incompletely digested macromolecules, lysosomes become large and numerous enough to interfere with normal
cell functions.
• There is a tight linkage between autophagy, mitochondrial function,
and lysosomes. As discussed in Chapter 2, a diverse range of cellular
organelles and molecules are degraded by autophagy including
complex lipids, polyubiquitinated proteins, mitochondria, and fragments of the endoplasmic reticulum. In particular, autophagy is essential for turnover of mitochondria, a process termed mitophagy.
Mitophagy serves as a quality control system whereby dysfunctional
mitochondria are degraded. Lysosomal enzyme defects lead to the
accumulation of undigested macromolecules in the lysosomes that
interfere with the processing of organelles delivered by autophago-cytic vacuoles, including mitochondria. As a result, damaged
mitochondria with poor calcium-buffering capacity and altered
membrane potentials persist and generate free radicals, releasing
molecules that trigger the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis. Impaired
autophagy also gives rise to secondary accumulation of autophagic
substrates including ubiquitinated and aggregation-prone polypeptides such as α-synuclein and Huntingtin protein (Chapter 1). This
provides a molecular link between neurodegenerative disorders and
lysosomal storage diseases such as Gaucher disease (discussed later).
There are three general approaches to the treatment of lysosomal
storage diseases. The most obvious is enzyme replacement, which may
take the form of cellular or gene therapies. Another approach, substrate reduction therapy, is based on the premise that if the substrate to
be degraded by the lysosomal enzyme can be reduced, the residual
enzyme activity may be sufficient to catabolize it and prevent accumulation. A third strategy is based on an understanding of the molecular
basis of enzyme deficiency. In many disorders, exemplified by Fabry
disease, the enzyme activity is low because the mutant proteins are
unstable and prone to misfolding and hence degraded in the endoplasmic reticulum. In such diseases, analogs of the enzyme substrate can
bind to the mutant enzyme and promote proper folding of the enzyme,
preventing its degradation and, paradoxically, restoring some activity.
This approach is termed molecular chaperone therapy.
Although the combined frequency of lysosomal storage disorders is
about 1 in 5000 live births, lysosomal dysfunction may be involved in
the etiology of several more common diseases. For example, an important genetic risk factor for developing Parkinson disease is the carrier
state for Gaucher disease, as virtually all patients with Gaucher disease
develop Parkinson disease. Niemann-Pick type C disease is another
lysosomal storage disorder that increases the risk for Alzheimer disease. Such interconnectedness stems from the multifunctionality of the
lysosome. For example, lysosomes play critical roles in (1) autophagy,
resulting from fusion with the autophagosome; (2) immunity, because
they fuse with phagosomes; and (3) membrane repair, through fusion
with the plasma membrane.
Approximately 70 lysosomal storage diseases have been identified.
These may result from abnormalities of lysosomal enzymes or proteins
involved in substrate degradation, endosomal sorting, or lysosomal
membrane integrity. Lysosomal storage disorders are divided into
categories based on the biochemical nature of the substrates and the
accumulated metabolites (Table 5.6). Within each group are several
entities, each resulting from deficiency of a specific enzyme.
In general, the distribution of the stored material, and hence the organs affected, is determined by two interrelated factors: (1) the tissue
where most of the material to be degraded is found and (2) the location
where most of the degradation normally occurs. For example, the brain
is rich in gangliosides, and hence defective hydrolysis of gangliosides, as
occurs in GM₁ and GM₂ gangliosidoses, results primarily in accumulation

An inherited deficiency of a functional lysosomal enzyme gives rise to
two pathologic consequences (Fig. 5.11).
• Catabolism of the substrate of the missing enzyme remains incomplete,
leading to the accumulation of the partially degraded insoluble

• There is a tight linkage between autophagy, mitochondrial function,
and lysosomes. As discussed in Chapter 2, a diverse range of cellular
organelles and molecules are degraded by autophagy including
complex lipids, polyubiquitinated proteins, mitochondria, and frag-
ments of the endoplasmic reticulum. In particular, autophagy is es-
sential for turnover of mitochondria, a process termed mitophagy.
Mitophagy serves as a quality control system whereby dysfunctional
mitochondria are degraded. Lysosomal enzyme defects lead to the
accumulation of undigested macromolecules in the lysosomes that
interfere with the processing of organelles delivered by autophago-
cytic vacuoles, including mitochondria. As a result, damaged
mitochondria with poor calcium-buffering capacity and altered
membrane potentials persist and generate free radicals, releasing
molecules that trigger the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis. Impaired
autophagy also gives rise to secondary accumulation of autophagic
substrates including ubiquitinated and aggregation-prone polypep-
tides such as a-synuclein and Huntingtin protein (Chapter 1). This
provides a molecular link between neurodegenerative disorders and
lysosomal storage diseases such as Gaucher disease (discussed later).
There are three general approaches to the treatment of lysosomal
storage diseases. The most obvious is enzyme replacement, which may
take the form of cellular or gene therapies. Another approach, sub-
strate reduction therapy, is based on the premise that if the substrate to
be degraded by the lysosomal enzyme can be reduced, the residual
enzyme activity may be sufficient to catabolize it and prevent accumu-
lation. A third strategy is based on an understanding of the molecular
basis of enzyme deficiency. In many disorders, exemplified by Fabry
disease, the enzyme activity is low because the mutant proteins are
unstable and prone to misfolding and hence degraded in the endoplas-
mic reticulum. In such diseases, analogs of the enzyme substrate can
bind to the mutant enzyme and promote proper folding of the enzyme,
preventing its degradation and, paradoxically, restoring some activity.
This approach is termed molecular chaperone therapy.
Although the combined frequency of lysosomal storage disorders is
about 1 in 5000 live births, lysosomal dysfunction may be involved in
the etiology of several more common diseases. For example, an impor-
tant genetic risk factor for developing Parkinson disease is the carrier
state for Gaucher disease, as virtually all patients with Gaucher disease
develop Parkinson disease. Niemann-Pick type C disease is another
lysosomal storage disorder that increases the risk for Alzheimer dis-
ease. Such interconnectedness stems from the multifunctionality of the
lysosome. For example, lysosomes play critical roles in (1) autophagy,
resulting from fusion with the autophagosome; (2) immunity, because
they fuse with phagosomes; and (3) membrane repair, through fusion
with the plasma membrane.
Approximately 70 lysosomal storage diseases have been identified.
These may result from abnormalities of lysosomal enzymes or proteins
involved in substrate degradation, endosomal sorting, or lysosomal
membrane integrity. Lysosomal storage disorders are divided into
categories based on the biochemical nature of the substrates and the
accumulated metabolites (Table 5.6). Within each group are several
entities, each resulting from deficiency of a specific enzyme.
In general, the distribution of the stored material, and hence the or-
gans affected, is determined by two interrelated factors: (1) the tissue
where most of the material to be degraded is found and (2) the location
where most of the degradation normally occurs. For example, the brain
is rich in gangliosides, and hence defective hydrolysis of gangliosides, as
occurs in GM₁ and GM₂ gangliosidoses, results primarily in accumulation

within neurons and consequent neurologic symptoms. Defects in degra-
dation  of  mucopolysaccharides  affect  virtually  every  organ  because
mucopolysaccharides are widely distributed in the body. Because cells of
the mononuclear phagocyte system are especially rich in lysosomes and
are involved in the degradation of a variety of substrates, organs rich in
phagocytic cells, such as the spleen and liver, are frequently enlarged in
several forms of lysosomal storage disorders. The ever-expanding num-
ber of lysosomal storage diseases can be divided into categories based on
the biochemical nature of the accumulated metabolite, thus creating
such subgroups as glycogenoses, sphingolipidoses (lipidoses), mucopolysac-
charidoses (MPSs), and mucolipidoses (see Table 5.6).
Most of these conditions are very rare. Only a few of the more com-
mon ones are considered here.
Tay-Sachs Disease (GM₂ Gangliosidosis: Hexosaminidase a-Subunit De-
ficiency).  GM₂ gangliosidoses are a group of three lysosomal storage
diseases  caused  by  deficiency  of  the  enzyme  β-hexosaminidase
resulting in an inability to catabolize GM₂ gangliosides. There are two
isoenzymes of β-hexosaminidase: Hex A, consisting of two subunits, a
and b, and Hex B, a homodimer of β-subunits. Degradation of GM₂ gan-
gliosides requires three polypeptides encoded by three distinct genes—
HEXA  (on  chromosome  15),  which  encodes  the  α-subunit  of  Hex
A; HEXB (on chromosome 5), which encodes the β-subunit of Hex A and
Hex B; and GM2A (on chromosome 5), which encodes an activator of
hexosaminidase. The phenotypic effects of mutations affecting these genes
are fairly similar because they result from accumulation of GM₂ ganglio-
sides. The underlying enzyme defect, however, is different for each. Tay-
Sachs disease, the most common form of GM₂ gangliosidosis, results from
mutations in the α-subunit locus on chromosome 15 that cause a severe
deficiency of hexosaminidase A. This disease is especially prevalent among
Jewish people, particularly among those of Eastern European (Ashkenazic)
origin, in whom a carrier rate of 1 in 30 has been reported.
The molecular basis for neuronal injury resulting from hexosa-
minidase deficiency is not fully understood. More than 100 mutations

CHAPTER 5 Genes and Human Diseases 137
have been described in the HEXA α-subunit gene; most affect protein
folding. Because the mutant protein is misfolded, it induces the so-called unfolded-protein response (Chapter 2). If such misfolded enzymes are not stabilized by chaperones, they undergo proteasomal
degradation, leading to accumulation of toxic substrates and intermediates within neurons. These findings have spurred clinical trials of
molecular chaperone therapy for some variants of later-onset Tay-
Sachs and other selected lysosomal storage diseases. Such therapy involves the use of synthetic chaperones that can cross the blood-brain
barrier, bind to the mutated protein, and enable its proper folding.
Sufficient functional enzyme can then be rescued to ameliorate the
effects of the inborn error.
MORPHOLOGY
GM₂ ganglioside accumulates in many tissues (e.g., heart, liver, spleen, nervous
system), but the involvement of neurons in the central and autonomic
nervous systems and retina dominate the clinical picture. On histologic
examination, the neurons are ballooned with cytoplasmic vacuoles, each representing a markedly distended lysosome filled with gangliosides (Fig. 5.12A).
With the electron microscope, several types of cytoplasmic inclusions can
be visualized, the most prominent being whorled configurations within lysosomes composed of onion-skin layers of membranes (Fig. 5.12B). In time there
is progressive destruction of neurons, proliferation of microglia, and accumulation of complex lipids in phagocytes within the brain substance. The ganglion
cells in the retina are similarly swollen with GM₂ ganglioside, particularly at the
margins of the macula. A cherry-red spot appears in the macula due to
accentuation of the normal color of the macular choroid contrasted with the
pallor produced by the swollen ganglion cells in the remainder of the retina
(Chapter 29). This finding is characteristic of Tay-Sachs disease and other storage disorders affecting the neurons.
Clinical Features
Affected infants appear normal at birth but begin to manifest signs and
symptoms at about age 6 months. There is relentless motor and mental
deterioration, leading eventually to muscular flaccidity and blindness.
Sometime during the early course of the disease, the characteristic, but
not pathognomonic, cherry-red spot appears in the macula of the eye
in almost all patients. Over the span of 1 or 2 years a complete vegetative state is reached, followed by death at age 2 to 3 years. Antenatal
diagnosis and carrier detection are possible by enzyme assays and
DNA-based analysis.
Niemann-Pick Disease Types A and B. Niemann-Pick disease types A
and B are two related disorders that are characterized by lysosomal
accumulation of sphingomyelin due to an inherited deficiency of
sphingomyelinase. Type A is a severe infantile form with extensive
neurologic involvement, marked visceral accumulations of sphingomyelin, progressive wasting, and early death within the first 3 years of life.
In contrast, patients with type B disease have organomegaly but generally no central nervous system involvement. Patients usually survive
into adulthood. As with Tay-Sachs disease, Niemann-Pick disease types
A and B are common in Ashkenazi Jewish populations. The gene for
acid sphingomyelinase maps to chromosome 11p15.4 and is one of the
imprinted genes that is preferentially expressed from the maternal chromosome because of epigenetic silencing of the paternal gene (discussed
later). Although this disease is typically inherited as an autosomal recessive, heterozygote carriers who inherit the mutant allele from their
mother can develop features of Niemann-Pick disease. More than 180
mutations have been found in the acid sphingomyelinase gene, and
specific mutations correlate with the severity of enzyme deficiency and
the associated clinical phenotype.
MORPHOLOGY
In the classic infantile type A variant, a missense mutation causes almost
complete deficiency of sphingomyelinase. Sphingomyelin is a ubiquitous component of cellular (including organellar) membranes, and so the enzyme deficiency blocks degradation of the lipid, resulting in its progressive accumulation
within lysosomes, particularly within cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system. Affected cells become enlarged, sometimes to 90 mm in diameter,
due to the distention of lysosomes with sphingomyelin and cholesterol. Innumerable small vacuoles of relatively uniform size are created, imparting foaminess to the cytoplasm (Fig. 5.13). Electron microscopy confirms
that the vacuoles are engorged secondary lysosomes that often contain
membranous cytoplasmic bodies resembling concentric lamellated myelin figures, sometimes called zebra bodies.
The lipid-laden phagocytic foam cells are widely distributed in the spleen,
liver, lymph nodes, bone marrow, tonsils, gastrointestinal tract, and lungs.
