CHAPTER 5 Genes and Human Diseases 159
parents have more than one affected child. This seemingly violates the laws
of Mendelian inheritance. Studies indicate that gonadal mosaicism is responsible for such unusual pedigrees. Such mosaicism results from a mutation that occurs postzygotically during early (embryonic) development. If
the mutation affects a cell lineage destined to form the gonads, the gametes
carry the mutation, but the somatic cells of the individual are completely
normal. A phenotypically normal parent who has gonadal mosaicism can
transmit the disease-causing mutation to the offspring through their mutated gametes. Because the progenitor cells of the gametes carry the mutation, there is a possibility that more than one child of such a parent will be
affected. The likelihood of such an occurrence depends on the proportion
of germ cells carrying the mutation. As mentioned earlier, risk for a small
group of disorders, including Apert syndrome (caused by FGFR2 mutations) and Costello syndrome (HRAS mutations), increase with paternal
age owing to positive selection for these mutations in the male germline.
Over the reproductive lifespan of males with gonadal mosaicism for these
mutations, representation of mutant sperm increase, as does the likelihood
of transmitting the mutation to an affected offspring.
Somatic Mosaicism
Mutations occur throughout the normal growth, development, and aging of tissues, and advances in sequencing technologies are enabling investigators to document baseline mutation rates and recurrent clonally
expanded mutations in various cell types. Many recurrent mutations
that contribute to the landscape of normal somatic mosaicism are potentially oncogenic, but in isolation they are insufficient to cause cancer.
Clonal hematopoiesis and histologic precursors of malignancies are
addressed in other chapters, as are interactions between somatically acquired “second hits” to tumor suppressor genes and germline mutations
that predispose to cancer (Chapter 7). Here, we briefly consider forms of
somatic mosaicism that present clinically as overgrowth syndromes.
A spectrum of somatic overgrowth disorders is recognized clinically,
including Proteus syndrome, CLOVES (congenital, lipomatous, overgrowth, vascular malformations, epidermal nevi, and spinal/skeletal
anomalies and/or scoliosis) syndrome, megalencephaly-polymicrogyria-polydactyly-hydrocephalus syndrome, and others. These are caused by de
novo (acquired) activating mutations in genes within the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PIK3CA)/AKT/ mechanistic target of rapamycin
(mTOR) pathway. PI3 kinases are cytoplasmic signaling molecules that
are recruited to phosphorylate phosphatidylinositol and phosphoinositide lipid substrates at the cell membrane when activated by growth factor
receptor tyrosine kinases. AKT and mTOR are critical downstream components of intracellular signaling pathways also activated by exogenous
growth factor signaling. In somatic overgrowth syndromes, activating
missense mutations in components of these pathways promote aberrant
pro-growth signaling even in the absence of exogenous growth factors.
Depending on the distribution of mutated cells during development (Fig. 5.32), different parts of the body are affected by asymmetric
overgrowth, which can involve bones, skin, and other tissues and organs, leading to regional differences in body size and growth rate.
Clinical trials are underway to identify optimal treatment with PI3K/
AKT/mTOR inhibitors, which in some circumstances are effective at-tenuators of progressive overgrowth.

parents have more than one affected child. This seemingly violates the laws

sponsible for such unusual pedigrees. Such mosaicism results from a muta-

carry the mutation, but the somatic cells of the individual are completely
normal. A phenotypically normal parent who has gonadal mosaicism can
transmit the disease-causing mutation to the offspring through their mu-

tions) and Costello syndrome (HRAS mutations), increase with paternal

Over the reproductive lifespan of males with gonadal mosaicism for these
mutations, representation of mutant sperm increase, as does the likelihood
of transmitting the mutation to an affected offspring.

Mutations occur throughout the normal growth, development, and ag-
ing of tissues, and advances in sequencing technologies are enabling in-
vestigators to document baseline mutation rates and recurrent clonally
expanded mutations in various cell types. Many recurrent mutations
that contribute to the landscape of normal somatic mosaicism are poten-
tially oncogenic, but in isolation they are insufficient to cause cancer.

addressed in other chapters, as are interactions between somatically ac-
quired “second hits” to tumor suppressor genes and germline mutations
that predispose to cancer (Chapter 7). Here, we briefly consider forms of
somatic mosaicism that present clinically as overgrowth syndromes.

including Proteus syndrome, CLOVES (congenital, lipomatous, over-
growth, vascular malformations, epidermal nevi, and spinal/skeletal
anomalies and/or scoliosis) syndrome, megalencephaly-polymicrogyria-

ide lipid substrates at the cell membrane when activated by growth factor

160 CHAPTER ₅  Genes and Human Diseases
conventional karyotyping for diagnosis of cytogenetic disorders (e.g.,
Down syndrome) and Southern blotting for the diagnosis of Hunting-
ton disease. Over time, a steady stream of technologic breakthroughs
has led to ever-increasing capabilities, particularly around nucleic acid
sequencing. These advances began with the development of Sanger
DNA sequencing in 1977 and PCR in 1983 and accelerated rapidly
with the advent of high throughput, massively parallel sequencing
strategies (often lumped together under the rubric next-generation
sequencing [NGS]) in the late 1990s. NGS has continued to improve in
terms of speed, cost, and read quality, and NGS-based testing is taking
a central role in the diagnosis and management of many diseases. That
said, certain types of genetic lesions are difficult to detect by short read
sequencing. The advent of long read sequencing technologies will
likely make complex structural rearrangements and mutations in re-
petitive genomic regions more accessible. An exhaustive discussion of
molecular diagnostics is beyond the scope of this book; here, we high-
light some of the most useful and widely deployed approaches.
When considering molecular genetic testing, it is important to re-
member that genetic markers can be either constitutional (i.e., present
in every cell of the affected person, as with a CFTR mutation in a pa-
tient with cystic fibrosis) or somatic (i.e., restricted to specific tissue
types or lesions, as with mutations in RAS in a variety of human can-
cers). These considerations determine the nature of the sample used
for the assay (e.g., peripheral blood cells, tumor tissue, nasopharyngeal
swab), and sequencing method (e.g., ensuring depth sufficient to re-
cover low variant allele frequencies).
Diagnostic Methods and Indications for Testing
There are many techniques and indications for performing molecular
genetic diagnostic tests on patient specimens. The burden of choice is
often problematic, both for molecular pathologists who design tests and
for clinicians who need to choose the optimal test for their patients.
Laboratory Considerations
Pathologists developing tests focus on the sensitivity, specificity, accu-
racy, and reproducibility of different methods as well as practical factors
like cost, labor, reliability, and turnaround time. To choose the most ap-
propriate diagnostic technique, one must have a thorough knowledge of
the spectrum of genetic anomalies that are responsible for the disease in
the patient population under study. Disease-causing genetic anomalies
range in size from single-base substitutions to gains or losses of entire
chromosomes and often vary widely in frequency among ethnic groups.
For example, standard cystic fibrosis testing for pathogenic mutations in
CFTR has a sensitivity of 94% in Ashkenazi Jewish populations, but
identifies less than 50% of affected patients in Asian populations. Hence,
proper test design requires careful consideration of these factors.  Fur-
thermore, in cases with negative standard test results and a high clinical
suspicion, further testing is indicated. However, even with extensive se-
quencing of CFTR, no pathogenic mutations are identified in approxi-
mately 10% of patients with classic cystic fibrosis; this is likely because
NGS assays miss certain genetic lesions (e.g., kilobase scale deletions and
gene rearrangements) that are better detected with other methods. Issues
like this arise frequently in genetic testing, and close communication
between primary care clinicians, medical genetics specialists, and diag-
nosticians is required to select the optimal test strategy in difficult cases.
Indications for Analysis of Inherited Genetic Alterations
Although it is not unusual for inherited genetic disorders to present in
adulthood, most testing is performed during the prenatal or postnatal/
childhood periods. Mendelian disorders caused by mutations in spe-
cific genes number in the thousands, and definitive diagnosis of most
of them is possible by DNA sequencing tests.
Other inherited disorders are the result of chromosomal aberra-
tions that usually present prenatally or at birth. Prenatal testing should
be offered for all fetuses at risk for a cytogenetic abnormality. Possible
indications include:
•  Advanced maternal age
•  A parent known to carry a balanced chromosomal rearrangement,
which greatly increases the frequency of abnormal chromosome
segregation during meiosis and the risk of aneuploidy in the zygote
•  Fetal anomalies observed on ultrasound
•  Routine maternal blood screening indicating an increased risk of
Down syndrome (trisomy 21) or another trisomy
Prenatal testing may also be considered for fetuses at known risk
for Mendelian disorders (e.g., cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy)
based on family history. At present, testing is usually performed on
cells obtained by amniocentesis, chorionic villus biopsy, or umbilical
cord blood. However, as much as 10% of the free DNA in a pregnant
mother’s blood is of fetal origin, and new sequencing technologies
have opened the door to an era of noninvasive prenatal diagnostics.
Following birth, testing is ideally done as soon as the possibility of
constitutional genetic disease arises. It is most commonly performed
on peripheral blood DNA and is targeted based on clinical suspicion.
In newborns or children, indications are:
•  Multiple congenital anomalies
•  Suspicion of a metabolic syndrome
•  Unexplained intellectual disability, and/or developmental delay
•  Suspected aneuploidy (e.g., features of Down syndrome) or other
syndromic chromosomal abnormality (e.g., deletions, inversions)
•  Suspected monogenic disease, whether previously described in the
family or new
In older patients, testing logically becomes more focused toward
genetic diseases that manifest at later stages of life. Again, the possi-
bilities are vast, but the more common indications include:
•  Inherited cancer syndromes (triggered by either family history or
an unusual cancer presentation, such as multiple cancer types or
unusually young age at diagnosis)
•  Atypically mild monogenic disease (e.g., attenuated cystic fibrosis)
•  Neurodegenerative  disorders  (e.g.,  familial  Alzheimer  disease,
Huntington disease)
Indications for Analysis of Acquired Genetic Alterations
In this era of molecularly targeted therapies, it is important to identify
mutations that inform treatment options in acquired diseases (e.g., cancer
and infectious disease). The technical approaches are the same as those
used for germline Mendelian disorders. Common indications include:
•  Diagnosis and management of cancer (Chapter 7)
•  Detection of tumor-specific mutations and cytogenetic altera-
tions that are the hallmarks of specific cancers (e.g., BCR-ABL
fusion genes in chronic myeloid leukemia [CML])
•  Determination of clonality as an indicator of a neoplastic condi-
tion (e.g., rearrangements of the immunoglobulin or T-cell re-
ceptor loci in lymphoid malignancies)
•  Identification  of  specific  genetic  alterations  that  can  direct
therapeutic choices (e.g., amplification of HER2 [official gene
name ERBB2] in breast cancer or mutation of EGFR [official
gene name ERBB1] in lung cancer)
•  Determination of treatment efficacy (e.g., minimal residual disease
detection in patients with CML by quantitative PCR for BCR-ABL)
•  Detection of drug-resistant secondary mutations in malignan-
cies treated with therapies that target specific proteins (e.g.,
mutated EGFR)

CHAPTER 5 Genes and Human Diseases 161
• Diagnosis and management of infectious disease (Chapter 8)
• Detection of microorganism-specific genetic material for definitive diagnosis (e.g., HIV, mycobacteria, human papillomavirus,
herpesvirus in central nervous system)
• Identification of alterations in microbial genomes that are associated with drug resistance
• Determination of treatment efficacy (e.g., assessment of viral
loads in HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, and hepatitis C virus infection)
PCR Detection of DNA and RNA Sequence Alterations
PCR analysis, which involves amplification of relatively short DNA
fragments from a DNA template, has been a mainstay of molecular
diagnostics for the last few decades. By using heat-stable DNA polymerases and thermal cycling to denature duplexed DNA and anneal
primers, the target DNA (usually ,1000 bp) lying between designed
primer sites is exponentially amplified from as little as one original
copy, greatly simplifying secondary sequence analysis. Many options
exist for subsequent analysis, each with different strengths and weak-nesses. A few of the more common options are:
• Sanger sequencing (Fig. 5.33). A single PCR product (amplicon) is
mixed with a DNA polymerase, a single primer, nucleotides, and
four dead-end (di-deoxy terminator) nucleotides (A, T, G, and C)
labeled with different fluorescent tags. The ensuing reaction produces a ladder of DNA molecules of all possible lengths, each labeled with a tag corresponding to the base at which the reaction
stopped due to incorporation of a terminator nucleotide. After size
separation by electrophoresis, the sequence is “read” and compared
with the normal sequence to detect mutations.
• Restriction fragment length analysis. This simple approach takes advantage of the digestion of DNA with endonucleases known as restriction enzymes that recognize and cut DNA at specific sequences.
If a specific mutation is known to affect a restriction enzyme cut site,
the amplified PCR product may be digested, and the normal and
mutant PCR products will yield fragments of different sizes that can
be easily distinguished by gel electrophoresis. This approach is targeted to specific, known nucleotide changes and considerably less
comprehensive than direct sequencing but remains useful for molecular diagnosis when the causal mutation is invariant.

CHAPTER ₅ Genes and Human Diseases 161
• Diagnosis and management of infectious disease (Chapter 8)
• Detection of microorganism-specific genetic material for defini-
tive diagnosis (e.g., HIV, mycobacteria, human papillomavirus,
herpesvirus in central nervous system)
• Identification of alterations in microbial genomes that are as-
sociated with drug resistance
• Determination of treatment efficacy (e.g., assessment of viral
loads in HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, and hepatitis C virus infection)
PCR Detection of DNA and RNA Sequence Alterations
PCR analysis, which involves amplification of relatively short DNA
fragments from a DNA template, has been a mainstay of molecular
diagnostics for the last few decades. By using heat-stable DNA poly-
merases and thermal cycling to denature duplexed DNA and anneal
primers, the target DNA (usually ,1000 bp) lying between designed
primer sites is exponentially amplified from as little as one original
copy, greatly simplifying secondary sequence analysis. Many options
exist for subsequent analysis, each with different strengths and weak-
nesses. A few of the more common options are:
• Sanger sequencing (Fig. 5.33). A single PCR product (amplicon) is
mixed with a DNA polymerase, a single primer, nucleotides, and
four dead-end (di-deoxy terminator) nucleotides (A, T, G, and C)
labeled with different fluorescent tags. The ensuing reaction pro-
duces a ladder of DNA molecules of all possible lengths, each la-
beled with a tag corresponding to the base at which the reaction
stopped due to incorporation of a terminator nucleotide. After size
separation by electrophoresis, the sequence is “read” and compared
with the normal sequence to detect mutations.
• Restriction fragment length analysis. This simple approach takes ad-
vantage of the digestion of DNA with endonucleases known as re-
striction enzymes that recognize and cut DNA at specific sequences.
If a specific mutation is known to affect a restriction enzyme cut site,
the amplified PCR product may be digested, and the normal and
mutant PCR products will yield fragments of different sizes that can
be easily distinguished by gel electrophoresis. This approach is tar-
geted to specific, known nucleotide changes and considerably less
comprehensive than direct sequencing but remains useful for mo-
lecular diagnosis when the causal mutation is invariant.

cloned genomic DNA spanning up to 200 kb are labeled with fluorescent dyes and applied to metaphase chromosome preparations or interphase nuclei that are pretreated so as to “melt” the genomic DNA.
The probe hybridizes to its homologous genomic sequence and thus
labels a specific chromosomal region that can be visualized by fluorescence microscopy. FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even
fixed archival tissue sections. It is used to detect numeric abnormalities
of chromosomes (aneuploidy) (see Fig. 5.21), microdeletions that are
not detectable by karyotyping (see Fig. 5.23) and variable partner
translocations or gene amplification (e.g., using MYC break-apart
probes which detect rearrangements with unknown partners or locus
amplifications). FISH can be used in certain circumstances when rapid
diagnosis is essential (e.g., when deciding to treat a patient with suspected acute promyelocytic leukemia with retinoic acid, which is effective only when a particular chromosomal translocation involving the
retinoic acid receptor gene is present in the tumor cells; Chapter 13).
Array Technology
FISH requires prior knowledge of the one or few specific chromosomal
regions suspected of being altered in the test sample. However, genomic
abnormalities can also be detected without prior knowledge by performing genome-wide surveys using microarray technology, whole-genome sequencing, or molecular imaging platforms. The first of
these is considered further here. First-generation microarray platforms
were designed for comparative genomic hybridization (CGH), while
newer platforms incorporate single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
genotyping approaches, offering multiple benefits.
• Array-based comparative genomic hybridization (CGH). In array
CGH, equal amounts of test DNA and a reference (normal) DNA
are labeled with two different fluorescent dyes (e.g., Cy3). The
samples are then mixed and hybridized to an array spotted with
DNA probes that span unique sequences in the human genome at
regularly spaced intervals. At each chromosomal probe location,
binding of the labeled DNA from the two samples is compared. If
the two samples are equal (i.e., the test sample is diploid), all spots
on the array will fluoresce yellow due to equal admixture of green
and red dyes. In contrast, if the test sample has a deletion or duplication, the probe spots corresponding to it will show skewing toward red or green (depending on gain or loss of material), allowing
highly accurate determination of even focal copy number gain or
loss anywhere across the genome. The smallest gains and losses that
can be detected depend on the density of the tiling probes (i.e., arrays with a probe placed every 200 base pairs will have greater
resolution for small gains and losses as compared with arrays with
a probe placed every kilobase), and usually several probes corresponding to contiguous genomic sequences need to be involved for
the interval gain or loss to be detected.
• Single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping arrays. Newer genomic
tiling arrays are based on a similar concept, but some or all of the
probes are designed to identify SNP sites genome-wide (i.e., a DNA
sample binds in a genotype-dependent manner), which provides a
number of advantages. As discussed in Chapter 1, SNPs are the most
common type of DNA polymorphism, occurring on average approximately every 1000 nucleotides throughout the genome. They
serve both as a physical landmark within the genome and as a genetic
marker whose transmission can be followed from parent to child.
There are several testing platforms using different methodologies that
allow SNPs to be analyzed genome-wide on arrays; details of these methods are beyond the scope of this discussion. Like CGH probes, these
methods involving SNPs can be used to make copy number variation
(CNV) calls, but by discriminating between SNP alleles at each particular
location they also provide genotype (haplotype) information (Fig. 5.34).

CHAPTER 5 Genes and Human Diseases 163
In the clinical laboratory, SNP arrays are routinely used to uncover copy number abnormalities in pediatric patients when the
karyotype is normal but a structural chromosomal abnormality is
still suspected. Common indications include congenital abnormalities, dysmorphic features, developmental delay, and autism. Notably,
unlike CGH arrays, SNP arrays can identify loss of heterozygosity. This
capability is important in the diagnosis of disorders caused by uniparental disomy (e.g., in Prader-Willi syndrome and Angelman syndrome), where, despite diploid genomic copy number, the SNP calls in
the affected chromosomal regions showed reduction to homozygosity.
Polymorphic Markers
Clinical detection of disease-specific mutations is possible only if the
gene responsible for the disorder is known and its sequence has been
identified. If the exact nature of the genetic aberration is not known, or
if testing for the primary defect is technically challenging or unfeasible,
diagnostic laboratories can take advantage of the phenomenon of linkage. In humans, two DNA loci neighboring one another on the same
chromosome are almost certain to cosegregate during meiosis due to
the extremely low chance of a crossover event happening between
them. Generally, the closer two loci are, the higher the probability that
they will travel together in family pedigrees; in some regions of the genome, linkage disequilibrium between two markers segregating in a
population can extend over long distances. In the event of a challenging
or unknown pathogenic allele, a diagnostic laboratory can sometimes
choose surrogate markers that travel together on the same strand and
“tag” the mutated sequence and use their presence to infer inheritance
of the mutated or normal allele in the context of the family pedigree.
The two types of genetic polymorphisms most useful for linkage
analysis are SNPs (described earlier) and repeat-length polymorphisms known as minisatellite and microsatellite repeats. Human
DNA contains short repetitive sequences of DNA giving rise to what are
called repeat-length polymorphisms. These polymorphisms are often
subdivided based on their length into microsatellite repeats and minisatellite repeats. Microsatellites are usually less than 1 kb and are characterized by a repeat size of 1 to 6 bp. Minisatellite repeats, by comparison,
are larger (1 to 3 kb), and the repeat motif is usually 10 to 100 bp. The
number of repeats, both in microsatellites and in minisatellites, can be
extremely variable within a given population, and hence these stretches
of DNA can be used to establish genetic identity. Most commonly,
minisatellites known as variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs) are
genotyped for this purpose, which involves PCR amplification using
primers that flank the repeat region. Fig. 5.35 depicts the application of
microsatellite linkage analysis to the PKD1 gene (historically very
difficult to sequence) for the familial diagnosis of adult polycystic kidney disease. In this example, the longest VNTR sequence is linked in
the family to the disease allele and can be used to track its transmission.
Assays to detect genetic polymorphisms are also important in
many other areas of medicine, including in the determination of
relatedness and identity in transplantation, paternity testing, and
forensic medicine. Since VNTR markers occur throughout the human genome and have such a high level of polymorphism, they are
ideal for differentiating between two individuals and to follow transmission of the marker from parent to child. Assays employing PCR
amplification of informative markers are now routinely used for
determining paternity and for criminal investigations. PCR can be
performed even with highly degraded biologic samples, allowing
DNA testing to play a central role in forensic identifications. The
same assays are used in patients following allogeneic hematopoietic
stem cell transplant to detect and quantify bone marrow chimerism,
which is evaluated by assessing the relative amounts of donor-derived and recipient-derived DNA.
Epigenetic Alterations
Epigenetics is defined as the study of chemical modification of DNA
or chromatin that do not alter the DNA sequence itself. As described
earlier, examples of such modifications include CpG dinucleotide
methylation of DNA and methylation and acetylation of histone proteins (Chapter 1). Diagnosis of an increasing number of diseases
involves the analysis of promoter methylation—for example, FXS, in
which hypermethylation results in FMR1 silencing. Methylation analysis is also essential in the diagnosis of Prader-Willi syndrome and
Angelman syndrome.
Special techniques are needed to detect DNA methylation. One approach is to treat genomic DNA with sodium bisulfite, a chemical that
converts unmethylated cytosine (C) to uracil (U), which acts like thy-mine (T) in downstream reactions. Methylated cytosines are protected
from modification and remain unchanged (C). After treatment, it is
then straightforward to discriminate the unmethylated (modified)
DNA from the methylated (unmodified) DNA by DNA sequencing.
Alternative approaches for assaying DNA methylation include
those that depend on proteins which selectively bind to methylated
DNA (e.g., enriching for DNA using methyl-CpG binding proteins) or
alter the DNA (e.g., using methylation sensitive restriction enzymes).
Still other methods recognize modified DNA bases directly, for example, based on changes in the kinetics of DNA polymerase copying a
template or methylation-specific changes in the ionic patterns produced as DNA strands are pulled through nanopore sequencers.

In the clinical laboratory, SNP arrays are routinely used to uncover copy number abnormalities in pediatric patients when the karyotype is normal but a structural chromosomal abnormality is still suspected. Common indications include congenital abnormalities, dysmorphic features, developmental delay, and autism. Notably, unlike CGH arrays, SNP arrays can identify loss of heterozygosity. This capability is important in the diagnosis of disorders caused by uniparental disomy (e.g., in Prader-Willi syndrome and Angelman syndrome), where, despite diploid genomic copy number, the SNP calls in the affected chromosomal regions showed reduction to homozygosity. Polymorphic Markers Clinical detection of disease-specific mutations is possible only if the gene responsible for the disorder is known and its sequence has been identified. If the exact nature of the genetic aberration is not known, or if testing for the primary defect is technically challenging or unfeasible, diagnostic laboratories can take advantage of the phenomenon of linkage. In humans, two DNA loci neighboring one another on the same chromosome are almost certain to cosegregate during meiosis due to the extremely low chance of a crossover event happening between them. Generally, the closer two loci are, the higher the probability that they will travel together in family pedigrees; in some regions of the genome, linkage disequilibrium between two markers segregating in a population can extend over long distances. In the event of a challenging or unknown pathogenic allele, a diagnostic laboratory can sometimes choose surrogate markers that travel together on the same strand and “tag” the mutated sequence and use their presence to infer inheritance of the mutated or normal allele in the context of the family pedigree. The two types of genetic polymorphisms most useful for linkage analysis are SNPs (described earlier) and repeat-length polymorphisms known as minisatellite and microsatellite repeats. Human DNA contains short repetitive sequences of DNA giving rise to what are called repeat-length polymorphisms. These polymorphisms are often subdivided based on their length into microsatellite repeats and minisatellite repeats. Microsatellites are usually less than 1 kb and are characterized by a repeat size of 1 to 6 bp. Minisatellite repeats, by comparison, are larger (1 to 3 kb), and the repeat motif is usually 10 to 100 bp. The number of repeats, both in microsatellites and in minisatellites, can be extremely variable within a given population, and hence these stretches of DNA can be used to establish genetic identity. Most commonly, minisatellites known as variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs) are genotyped for this purpose, which involves PCR amplification using primers that flank the repeat region. Fig. 5.35 depicts the application of microsatellite linkage analysis to the PKD1 gene (historically very difficult to sequence) for the familial diagnosis of adult polycystic kidney disease. In this example, the longest VNTR sequence is linked in the family to the disease allele and can be used to track its transmission. Assays to detect genetic polymorphisms are also important in many other areas of medicine, including in the determination of relatedness and identity in transplantation, paternity testing, and forensic medicine. Since VNTR markers occur throughout the human genome and have such a high level of polymorphism, they are ideal for differentiating between two individuals and to follow transmission of the marker from parent to child. Assays employing PCR amplification of informative markers are now routinely used for determining paternity and for criminal investigations. PCR can be performed even with highly degraded biologic samples, allowing DNA testing to play a central role in forensic identifications. The same assays are used in patients following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant to detect and quantify bone marrow chimerism, which is evaluated by assessing the relative amounts of donor-derived and recipient-derived DNA. Epigenetic Alterations Epigenetics is defined as the study of chemical modification of DNA or chromatin that do not alter the DNA sequence itself. As described earlier, examples of such modifications include CpG dinucleotide methylation of DNA and methylation and acetylation of histone proteins (Chapter 1). Diagnosis of an increasing number of diseases involves the analysis of promoter methylation—for example, FXS, in which hypermethylation results in FMR1 silencing. Methylation analysis is also essential in the diagnosis of Prader-Willi syndrome and Angelman syndrome.

Special techniques are needed to detect DNA methylation. One approach is to treat genomic DNA with sodium bisulfite, a chemical that converts unmethylated cytosine (C) to uracil (U), which acts like thy-mine (T) in downstream reactions. Methylated cytosines are protected from modification and remain unchanged (C). After treatment, it is then straightforward to discriminate the unmethylated (modified) DNA from the methylated (unmodified) DNA by DNA sequencing. Alternative approaches for assaying DNA methylation include those that depend on proteins which selectively bind to methylated DNA (e.g., enriching for DNA using methyl-CpG binding proteins) or alter the DNA (e.g., using methylation sensitive restriction enzymes). Still other methods recognize modified DNA bases directly, for example, based on changes in the kinetics of DNA polymerase copying a template or methylation-specific changes in the ionic patterns produced as DNA strands are pulled through nanopore sequencers. 164 CHAPTER 5 Genes and Human Diseases
Next-Generation Sequencing
Next-generation sequencing is a term used to describe several newer
DNA sequencing technologies that produce very large amounts of
sequence data in a massively parallel manner. These technologies
have revolutionized biomedical research and molecular diagnostics.
The factors propelling rapid adoption of NGS are price and throughput: NGS allows us to perform otherwise impossibly comprehensive
(e.g., covering all exons) or “deep” (high coverage) analyses at extremely low cost.
One feature that makes NGS far more clinically applicable than
Sanger sequencing is its input sample requirement. Whereas Sanger
sequencing requires a single homogeneous template DNA (usually a
specific PCR product), NGS has no such requirement: any DNA from
almost any source can be used. Because Sanger sequencing essentially
provides an “average” result for a particular DNA region in a sample,
samples with substantial sequence heterogeneity among input DNA
molecules produce uninterpretable results. NGS, by contrast, is well
suited to analysis of heterogeneous DNA samples due to the application of three common basic principles (Fig. 5.36).
• Spatial separation. At the beginning of the procedure, individual
DNA molecules are physically isolated from each other in space.
The specifics of this process are platform dependent.
• Local amplification. After separation, the individual DNA molecules are amplified in place using a limited number of PCR cycles.
Amplification is necessary so that sufficient signal can be generated
to ensure detection and accuracy.

• Parallel sequencing. The amplified DNA molecules are then simultaneously sequenced by the addition of polymerases and other re-agents, with each spatially separated and amplified original molecule
yielding a “read” corresponding to its sequence. Sequence reads from
NGS instruments are generally short, less than 500 bp.
Bioinformatics
Each NGS analysis generates a staggering amount of sequence data; for
high throughput sequencing instruments, this amounts to billions of
DNA reads and terabytes (Tb) of data per day, enough to produce a
high-quality sequence spanning an entire human genome. The downstream analysis is sufficiently complex that specialized training in
bioinformatics is needed. Computational “pipelines” vary widely
across applications and sample types, and a detailed discussion is beyond the scope of this text. However, it is worth describing the basic
steps necessary to process this type of data.
• Alignment. Alignment is the process by which the sequencing reads
from a sample are mapped to a reference genome, allowing them to
be viewed and interpreted in context.
• Variant calling. This process involves a systematic comparison of
the sequence data from a sample with the reference sequence.
Samples are typically sequenced to sufficient coverage that germline
polymorphisms in the target intervals are identified. The more
reads that cover a particular location (sequencing depth), the more
likely that variants with low variant allele frequency (VAF) in a
sample will be detected.

Next-Generation Sequencing

Next-generation sequencing is a term used to describe several newer DNA sequencing technologies that produce very large amounts of sequence data in a massively parallel manner. These technologies have revolutionized biomedical research and molecular diagnostics. The factors propelling rapid adoption of NGS are price and throughput: NGS allows us to perform otherwise impossibly comprehensive (e.g., covering all exons) or “deep” (high coverage) analyses at extremely low cost. One feature that makes NGS far more clinically applicable than Sanger sequencing is its input sample requirement. Whereas Sanger sequencing requires a single homogeneous template DNA (usually a specific PCR product), NGS has no such requirement: any DNA from almost any source can be used. Because Sanger sequencing essentially provides an “average” result for a particular DNA region in a sample, samples with substantial sequence heterogeneity among input DNA molecules produce uninterpretable results. NGS, by contrast, is well suited to analysis of heterogeneous DNA samples due to the application of three common basic principles (Fig. 5.36).
• Spatial separation. At the beginning of the procedure, individual DNA molecules are physically isolated from each other in space. The specifics of this process are platform dependent.

• Local amplification. After separation, the individual DNA molecules are amplified in place using a limited number of PCR cycles. Amplification is necessary so that sufficient signal can be generated to ensure detection and accuracy.

• Parallel sequencing. The amplified DNA molecules are then simultaneously sequenced by the addition of polymerases and other re-agents, with each spatially separated and amplified original molecule yielding a “read” corresponding to its sequence. Sequence reads from NGS instruments are generally short, less than 500 bp. Bioinformatics Each NGS analysis generates a staggering amount of sequence data; for high throughput sequencing instruments, this amounts to billions of DNA reads and terabytes (Tb) of data per day, enough to produce a high-quality sequence spanning an entire human genome. The downstream analysis is sufficiently complex that specialized training in bioinformatics is needed. Computational “pipelines” vary widely across applications and sample types, and a detailed discussion is beyond the scope of this text. However, it is worth describing the basic steps necessary to process this type of data.
• Alignment. Alignment is the process by which the sequencing reads from a sample are mapped to a reference genome, allowing them to be viewed and interpreted in context.

• Variant calling. This process involves a systematic comparison of the sequence data from a sample with the reference sequence. Samples are typically sequenced to sufficient coverage that germline polymorphisms in the target intervals are identified. The more reads that cover a particular location (sequencing depth), the more likely that variants with low variant allele frequency (VAF) in a sample will be detected.

CHAPTER 5 Genes and Human Diseases 165
• Variant annotation and interpretation. Variants can be annotated
with various pieces of information (e.g., gene name, coding change
and protein effect predictions, information from databases listing
commonly occurring as well as pathogenic variants, clinical information). Once reviewed by the clinical laboratory, the annotated
data are ready for reporting. Because the pace of advances in genetics and genomics has far outpaced the knowledge of the typical
clinician, an important part of this report is a brief description of
the biological and clinical significance of each pathogenic variant,
which can be numerous in the case of some cancers.
• Mutational signature calling. In addition to totaling up individual
mutations, informatics algorithms have been developed that detect
patterns of mutations that point to particular environmental exposures (e.g., ultraviolet light, smoking) or underlying defects in DNA
repair. These have become clinically relevant with the discovery that
cancers with high tumor mutational burden (TMB) or acquired defects in mismatch repair genes that lead to microsatellite instability
(MSI) tend to be responsive to immune checkpoint inhibitors (Chapter 7). Based on this observation, many clinical laboratories are now
“calling” the TMB and MSI status of cancers based on NGS results.
Clinical Applications of Next-Generation DNA Sequencing
As discussed, any DNA sample can be analyzed by NGS. However, the
DNA needs to first be prepared for sequencing by constructing a library of short DNA sequences that are enriched for genomic regions of
interest (e.g., particular exons or the “whole exome”). There are several
methods for NGS library preparation from genomic DNA. In the
clinical laboratories, most applications of NGS are targeted toward
constitutional genetic disease and cancer diagnostics, using a few different basic approaches:
• Targeted sequencing. Most current clinical laboratory NGS tests fall
in this category. Targeted sequencing is focused on the exons of a
carefully selected panel of genes, which maximizes sequencing
depth while minimizing costs and the time and expense required
for interpretation and clinical reporting. Sample preparation for
targeted sequencing is typically performed by enriching sequences
in an NGS library by hybrid capture using a panel of synthesized
biotinylated probes complementary to the regions of interest. Single-gene NGS assays for inherited disorders are also becoming
more common, and many laboratories that previously performed
costly Sanger sequencing of multiple PCR products (i.e., to enable
comprehensive CFTR sequencing) are now moving these assays to
NGS platforms. Targeted NGS with gene panels is also now com-monplace in evaluating individuals with genetic diseases such as
cardiomyopathy and congenital deafness. In cancer testing, gene
panels are widely used to perform detailed tumor profiling. Each
tumor has a unique set of somatic mutations, and these assays aim
to detect as many treatable or prognostic mutations as possible to
offer individually tailored patient care. Increasingly, repeat testing
at the time of disease recurrence is also being performed to understand mechanisms of drug resistance, which can serve to guide the
selection of second-line therapies.
• Whole-exome sequencing (WES). WES is a more expansive type of
targeted sequencing, in which hundreds of thousands of probes are
used to enrich for the roughly 1.5% of the genome that consists of
protein-encoding exons prior to NGS. It has led to some success
stories in identifying the molecular basis for constitutional genetic
diseases, allowing physicians to deliver answers and even therapies
for children with orphan diseases who had suffered through prolonged and unsuccessful diagnostic odysseys. WES is also used in
oncology, mostly in the research setting to discover alterations in
infrequently mutated genes.
• Whole-genome sequencing (WGS). WGS is the most comprehensive type of DNA analysis that can be performed on an individual.
Current indications for use in medical genetics are mostly limited
to cases where exome sequencing has failed to provide an answer,
but the clinical suspicion of genetic disease remains high. For
cancer applications, WGS of sufficient depth can detect noncoding mutations and novel structural rearrangements (e.g., insertions, deletions, translocations) that may be clinically relevant,
but relatively high costs, slow turnaround times, and significant
informatics challenges still preclude its routine use in clinical
practice.
Liquid Biopsies and ctDNA Analysis
Because NGS can provide information from few starting molecules
and can detect infrequent alleles in admixtures of normal and abnormal DNA, it is opening a field of cancer biomarker detection in the
peripheral blood. In some clinical scenarios, relatively noninvasive
blood draws (being termed “liquid biopsies”) can recover sufficient
material shed from tumor cells and provide information that previously required direct surgical sampling (Fig. 5.37). Genomic DNA
from tumors can exist in the blood both in circulating tumor cells that
detach from solid tumor site(s) or “free” in the circulation, released by
dead or dying cells.

Genomic DNA can exist in circulating tumor cells or can be “free” in the

• Variant annotation and interpretation. Variants can be annotated with various pieces of information (e.g., gene name, coding change and protein effect predictions, information from databases listing commonly occurring as well as pathogenic variants, clinical information). Once reviewed by the clinical laboratory, the annotated data are ready for reporting. Because the pace of advances in genetics and genomics has far outpaced the knowledge of the typical clinician, an important part of this report is a brief description of the biological and clinical significance of each pathogenic variant, which can be numerous in the case of some cancers.

• Mutational signature calling. In addition to totaling up individual mutations, informatics algorithms have been developed that detect patterns of mutations that point to particular environmental exposures (e.g., ultraviolet light, smoking) or underlying defects in DNA repair. These have become clinically relevant with the discovery that cancers with high tumor mutational burden (TMB) or acquired defects in mismatch repair genes that lead to microsatellite instability (MSI) tend to be responsive to immune checkpoint inhibitors (Chapter 7). Based on this observation, many clinical laboratories are now “calling” the TMB and MSI status of cancers based on NGS results. Clinical Applications of Next-Generation DNA Sequencing As discussed, any DNA sample can be analyzed by NGS. However, the DNA needs to first be prepared for sequencing by constructing a library of short DNA sequences that are enriched for genomic regions of interest (e.g., particular exons or the “whole exome”). There are several methods for NGS library preparation from genomic DNA. In the clinical laboratories, most applications of NGS are targeted toward constitutional genetic disease and cancer diagnostics, using a few different basic approaches:

• Targeted sequencing. Most current clinical laboratory NGS tests fall in this category. Targeted sequencing is focused on the exons of a carefully selected panel of genes, which maximizes sequencing depth while minimizing costs and the time and expense required for interpretation and clinical reporting. Sample preparation for targeted sequencing is typically performed by enriching sequences in an NGS library by hybrid capture using a panel of synthesized biotinylated probes complementary to the regions of interest. Single-gene NGS assays for inherited disorders are also becoming more common, and many laboratories that previously performed costly Sanger sequencing of multiple PCR products (i.e., to enable comprehensive CFTR sequencing) are now moving these assays to NGS platforms. Targeted NGS with gene panels is also now com-monplace in evaluating individuals with genetic diseases such as cardiomyopathy and congenital deafness. In cancer testing, gene panels are widely used to perform detailed tumor profiling. Each tumor has a unique set of somatic mutations, and these assays aim to detect as many treatable or prognostic mutations as possible to offer individually tailored patient care. Increasingly, repeat testing at the time of disease recurrence is also being performed to understand mechanisms of drug resistance, which can serve to guide the selection of second-line therapies.

• Whole-exome sequencing (WES). WES is a more expansive type of targeted sequencing, in which hundreds of thousands of probes are used to enrich for the roughly 1.5% of the genome that consists of protein-encoding exons prior to NGS. It has led to some success stories in identifying the molecular basis for constitutional genetic diseases, allowing physicians to deliver answers and even therapies for children with orphan diseases who had suffered through prolonged and unsuccessful diagnostic odysseys. WES is also used in oncology, mostly in the research setting to discover alterations in infrequently mutated genes.

• Whole-genome sequencing (WGS). WGS is the most comprehensive type of DNA analysis that can be performed on an individual. Current indications for use in medical genetics are mostly limited to cases where exome sequencing has failed to provide an answer, but the clinical suspicion of genetic disease remains high. For cancer applications, WGS of sufficient depth can detect noncoding mutations and novel structural rearrangements (e.g., insertions, deletions, translocations) that may be clinically relevant, but relatively high costs, slow turnaround times, and significant informatics challenges still preclude its routine use in clinical practice.
Liquid Biopsies and ctDNA Analysis

Because NGS can provide information from few starting molecules and can detect infrequent alleles in admixtures of normal and abnormal DNA, it is opening a field of cancer biomarker detection in the peripheral blood. In some clinical scenarios, relatively noninvasive blood draws (being termed “liquid biopsies”) can recover sufficient material shed from tumor cells and provide information that previously required direct surgical sampling (Fig. 5.37). Genomic DNA from tumors can exist in the blood both in circulating tumor cells that detach from solid tumor site(s) or “free” in the circulation, released by dead or dying cells.
Circulating tumor cell ctDNA Apoptotic cell Tumor Extracellular vesicles Point mutation Methylation changes

Fig. 5.37 Liquid biopsies and analyses of circulating DNA. Innovations in diagnostics are revealing analytes in the peripheral blood that are derived from tumors. This enables relatively noninvasive blood draws, so-called liquid biopsies, to sample cancerous material and provide information that previously required surgical collections of tumor tissue. Genomic DNA can exist in circulating tumor cells or can be “free” in the circulation (circulating tumor, ctDNA). Next-generation sequencing (NGS) analyses allow for the detection of point mutations and methylation changes that can provide information about the burden of disease and tumor type. Other highly sensitive assays to detect trace proteins and extracellular vesicles (exosomes) extruded from malignant cells may compliment these approaches.

166 CHAPTER ₅  Genes and Human Diseases
Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is recognizable as abnormal either
because of the presence of recurrent cancer-driving point mutations,
the presence of “passenger mutations” inherent to an individual’s tumor
(creating a “bespoke” mutation signature unique to that patient), or the
existence of epigenetic alterations associated with malignancy. Because
DNA methylation patterns are highly dependent on cell types, epigen-
etic signatures can be used not only to indicate the presence of a cancer,
but also can inform its origin. Other highly sensitive assays are being
applied to detect trace proteins and tumor cell extracellular vesicles
(exosomes) which may compliment ctDNA analyses.
This is a very active area of investigation and innovation in cancer
diagnostics, where there are significant needs for biomarkers: (1) to
improve detection of early stage, and thus more treatable malignancies;
(2) to reduce false positives, false negatives, and the expense of would-
be screening tests; (3) to predict and monitor therapeutic responses;
and (4) to indicate persistence of minimal residual disease to inform
therapeutic decision-making.

Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is recognizable as abnormal either because of the presence of recurrent cancer-driving point mutations, the presence of “passenger mutations” inherent to an individual’s tumor

(creating a “bespoke” mutation signature unique to that patient), or the existence of epigenetic alterations associated with malignancy. Because DNA methylation patterns are highly dependent on cell types, epigenetic signatures can be used not only to indicate the presence of a cancer, but also can inform its origin. Other highly sensitive assays are being applied to detect trace proteins and tumor cell extracellular vesicles
(exosomes) which may compliment ctDNA analyses.

This is a very active area of investigation and innovation in cancer diagnostics, where there are significant needs for biomarkers: (1) to improve detection of early stage, and thus more treatable malignancies;

(2) to reduce false positives, false negatives, and the expense of would-be screening tests; (3) to predict and monitor therapeutic responses; and (4) to indicate persistence of minimal residual disease to inform therapeutic decision-making.
